World.title: A celebration of Mexican artist Arturo García Bustos, 100 years after his birth
World.content:
On Aug. 8, 1926, a child was born in the heart of Mexico City. Although he grew up to explore many places, his heart remained where his passion for art was first sparked, and he passed away in his house in Coyoacán on April 7, 2017.

Arturo García Bustos is recognized for his role in Mexican art history, notably as a student of Frida Kahlo and a dedicated artist whose legacy continues to inspire.

“The love that Frida instilled in us towards Mexican culture, towards our roots and popular customs, is still alive and present in my work,” the artist stated in a 1977 interview with El Día, underscoring his lifelong dedication to Mexican identity.

A childhood in the city

One cannot grow up in Mexico City without it leaving a mark. García Bustos was well aware of this, recalling fondly that as a primary school student, he would watch Diego Rivera working on his murals at the Secretaría de Educación Pública (Ministry of Public Education).

Little did he know that he would eventually marry one of Rivera’s close collaborators, Rina Lazo, and become closer to the master muralist than he could have ever imagined.

Living downtown put him at the center of a growing metropolis, where he attended public concerts, frequented local libraries and developed a keen eye for observing urban life.

A rebellious spirit

Ever the rebel, García Bustos broke away from the strict, rigid norms of the Academia de San Carlos, Mexico’s most prestigious art academy at the time. He transferred to La Esmeralda — a decision that altered his life forever. There, he not only found his true mentors, but also met Guatemalan-Mexican artist Rina Lazo, the woman he would marry and spend his life alongside.

In contrast with the San Carlos Academy, Frida Kahlo didn’t teach through theory. She avoided a clinical approach to creation, favoring a sensitive, vibrant perspective on the artistic process instead.

She challenged her students to observe the world deeply, asking them to count the subtle colors hidden in everyday objects. When her failing health made her commute to La Esmeralda impossible, she transformed her beloved Casa Azul in Coyoacán into a creative sanctuary. It was here that Arturo García Bustos became one of the four devoted pupils known as “Los Fridos.”

Kahlo’s mentorship catalyzed a breakthrough that launched García Bustos into the Mexican art scene. Kahlo actively championed her students’ careers, securing them local mural projects — like painting the walls of a nearby pulquería — and introducing their work to leading Mexican intellectuals.

García Bustos, the militant

La Esmeralda also connected Arturo to artist collectives that defined the trajectory of his work: the Taller de Gráfica Popular (TGP) and Artistas Jóvenes Revolucionarios. These groups were not merely social clubs; they were part of a broader movement given voice by printmakers and painters who proudly viewed themselves as visual working-class laborers.

Bustos quickly adopted graphic art as one of his primary media. At just 18 years old, he joined the Taller de Gráfica Popular — founded by Leopoldo Méndez, Luis Arenal and Pablo O’Higgins — to design flyers, posters and newspapers that documented global struggles and amplified labor union demands.

Through the TGP, García Bustos deepened his understanding of both printmaking and sociopolitical activism. Members divided their time equally between pulling prints and attending political assemblies or protests, bridging the gap between art and labor.

Simultaneously, young creators were forging their own spaces. The Artistas Jóvenes Revolucionarios collective brought together students seeking to display politically engaged artwork. Bypassing traditional galleries and museums, they exhibited in public parks and markets to invite direct dialogue with everyday citizens.

Inevitably, a teacher

Following in Kahlo’s footsteps, Arturo dedicated years of his life to education. Two institutions stand out in his teaching journey: the Escuela Nacional de Artes Plásticas in Guatemala and the Escuela de Bellas Artes de Oaxaca.

He was invited to Guatemala by writer and diplomat Luis Cardoza y Aragón — a move warmly supported by his wife, Rina Lazo. During his residency, he established a printmaking workshop that produced socially critical work, though political upheaval soon forced him to return to Mexico.

García Bustos shaped generations of talent, including renowned artist Francisco Toledo, through his dedicated work at the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Oaxaca, inspiring respect for his mentorship.

Artwork

There are two remarkable paths that García Bustos followed — or rather cultivated — throughout his career: muralism and printmaking. Perhaps at first sight they may seem far from one another, but they shared a common interest in getting art to the people. While the former is usually displayed publicly, the latter is, by nature, easy to reproduce repeatedly.

Regarding the first discipline, more than 10 murals can be attributed — individually or collectively — to García Bustos. His motifs always revolve around Mexican history, Indigenous traditions and social justice. Although all his work has been equally relevant, certain pieces have sparked debate and become landmarks where they were created.

In Oaxaca

One of his most significant murals, “Las Siete Regiones de Oaxaca,” created for the National Museum of Anthropology, exemplifies his dedication to Mexican history and cultural identity.

When Arturo created the murals for the Palacio de Gobierno de Oaxaca in 1980, there was much discussion about whether a non-Oaxacan artist should paint them; one of the main opponents was Oaxacan artist Rufino Tamayo. The protests eventually ceased once supporters argued that García Bustos had already given a great deal to the state through his teaching at the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Oaxaca.

In Mexico City

Additionally, he painted a stunning mural that thousands of people see every day at the Metro station Universidad in Mexico City, located at the heart of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México: “The University on the Threshold of the 21st Century.” In this piece, Arturo journeys through the different means of knowledge and education in Mexico. He also portrays key historical figures such as Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, his mentor Frida Kahlo and his lifelong partner, Rina Lazo.

Finally, one of his last murals adorns the walls of the Casa de Cultura de Azcapotzalco in Mexico City. Here, García Bustos not only showcases his technical expertise but also enriches a community cultural space with iconic moments from Mexican history.

On the 100th anniversary of his birth, Arturo García Bustos has become an undeniably influential figure in modern Mexican art, far beyond his status as one of Los Fridos. Ultimately, his legacy enriches Mexico’s public spaces and the generations of artists he inspired alongside Rina Lazo.

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: Beyond the lechero: Veracruz’s new wave of coffee culture
World.content:
When I first decided to leave the San Francisco Bay Area in California to live in Xalapa, Veracruz — the city where both of my parents once immigrated from decades ago, and where my mom eventually moved back to live — I never anticipated how much I would fall in love with one of Mexico’s best-kept secrets: Jarocho coffee.

The state’s adoration for, and history of, producing some of Mexico’s best coffee dates back centuries. This is, after all, where coffee cultivation began with the arrival of Europeans in the 1700s. While living here, I’ve been able to travel along the oldest coffee-producing trails on the continent, sipping my way through it all, and visiting coffee plantations to learn more about the process and conditions for cultivating coffee and its environmental impacts in modern times (spoiler: it’s harder than ever for producers to keep up with the global demand and maintain their practices from the past).

The rich coffee culture of Veracruz

In Mexico’s entirety, no state boasts the same pedigree of rich coffee lineage and ongoing traditions as deeply, and perhaps as invisibly, as Veracruz. Nowhere is that notion more evident than in the state’s largest city: the actual port itself.

Of course, Jarocho coffee is by no means completely unheard of or brand new, by any stretch of the imagination, particularly for those in the know. The sight of a “lechero” pouring frothy milk into a cup of espresso at El Gran Café de la Parroquia is a classic image of the Veracruz experience going back to 1808, when the cafe first opened as a tiny operation in front of the Parroquia de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción.

Now, it represents one of Mexico’s most iconic coffee rituals. Here’s how it works: patrons tap their glass with a spoon; a formally dressed lechero comes bustling over with a steaming pot of milk; the lechero evinces showmanship by pouring the milk from a spout at an impressive height, never spilling a drop. It may seem gimmicky for some, but throughout my life, it has always represented the Jarocho way of drinking coffee.

Café traditionalism

In addition to El Gran Café de la Parroquia (which eventually split into two separate factions due to ownership disputes in the 1990s), Gran Café del Portal in Veracruz’s historic center is also worth visiting for its colonial-era charm and sense of coffee traditionalism. Indeed, the port of Veracruz’s reputational coffee heritage has carried over into other parts of Mexico over the years, too; the most popular café in Coyoacán is named El Jarocho, which opened in 1953, and ships its coffee beans by the truckloads directly from Huatusco, Veracruz.

And yet, while becoming an intrinsic part of a classic tourist experience in Veracruz, the city has not always found a way to merge its glorious coffee past with its ongoing present and future. Until now.

A new generation of cafés

Currently, the specialty coffee scene in the port of Veracruz is booming in unseen ways, as a new wave of coffeemakers and baristas has entered the mix with a more contemporary approach, offering a cool range of Veracruz’s flavorful past in an aesthetic, renovated context. In just the past year and a half that I’ve lived in the state of Veracruz, I’ve noticed an uptick of youthful cafés in the puerto; it seems that every time I go for a weekend outing with my family, another one springs up.

So here are just a few of those cafes that should be added to your list. The next time you decide to visit Mexico’s oldest and most historically important port city — where imbibing a cup of coffee in the midday swelter is a way of life — you can experience its coffee renaissance for yourself.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Singular Coffee Roasters (@singular.coffee.roasters)

Located directly across the street from Playa de Oro, right on the border of Boca del Rio — a ritzier suburb a few miles away from the industrial center of Veracruz — Singular Coffee Roasters in many ways embodies the next generation of coffeemakers in the city. In addition to having a pristine view of the beach, where the nearby ocean scenically blows palm trees along the main avenue, the vibe is funky and hip, and the menu is top-notch.

Enjoy a tampiqueña de res (a thin cut of beef served with salsa, salad greens and beans) alongside an orange cold brew, a maracuyita (cold brew mixed with mashed passion fruit) or a matcha frappe. Or, keep it simple, and order a locally sourced cup of filtered coffee — with the option of adding coconut milk for an extra 20 pesos. Either way, it’ll be a refreshing way to start off your day before hitting the nearby Gulf’s waters to cool off from the oppressive weight of the year-round heat.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by IMPETUS – Casa Tostadora de Café (@impetus.mx)

With three locations sprinkled throughout the city, Impetus has become the “it” café in town. Recently named as one of seven finalists in Mexico’s nationwide Expo Café, the brand is certainly of the highest caliber, and the interior decor and design of each café matches the high-grade taste in each cup. Though their original location has been around for 10 years now, they’ve still retained the title as Veracruz’s leading specialty coffee purveyors with a seasonally changing menu. Available in multiple price tiers ascending from lowest to highest (coffee of the day, excellent or extraordinary), they’re known for their fine-tuned brewing methods. In true Veracruz fashion, you can cool off with a granizado de olla (shaved ice poured over with café de olla) or a chilled bottle of housemade cascarita (a fruity, tea-like beverage made by steeping the dried husks of a coffee cherry in water).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ETHOS Casa de Café (@ethos_casadecafe)

Small but mighty, this bite-sized café (it’s a small room that comfortably seats around 10 people, not counting the limited sidewalk seating available outside) was named as one of the Top 100 Coffee Shops in North America, Central America and the Caribbean islands. Aside from their regular pours — which are exceptional — they offer cold brews infused with in-house ginger ale, coffee liqueur frappes and dulce de leche espressos, among other inventive options like the Blue Velvet (a concoction of blue butterfly pea flower extract, lavender, organic vanilla and milk).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by VOLADOR – Café de Altura (@volador.mx)

Recognized as a two-time Expo Café winner for producing the best coffee in Mexico, this outpost can be found on a vibrant strip in Colonia Reforma (which, for my money, is the coolest and most diverse neighborhood in the state of Veracruz, replete with stylish bars, cafés, taquerias, Korean ramen, smash burgers, Middle Eastern dining, pizzerias and more, all connected by a tree-lined walking path that leads straight to the beach). Volador is the unequivocal king of coffee in this area, with a spacious environment and outdoor patio seating to accompany its vegan food options, salads and — for the over-18 crowd — carajillos (espresso and coffee liqueur) in mazapan or horchata varietals.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Avi Café (@avicafe_)

Specializing in brunch and sweet treats — in addition to their selection of coffee and teas — this dog-friendly café is charming and sprightly. Another of Colonia Reforma’s highlights, it opened at the end of 2024 and has added to Veracruz’s rising cafe presence. A pistachio tarta vasca (a dense Basque-style cheesecake) is ideally partnered with a tri-colored strawberry matcha, an iced taro or a classic espresso cortado.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @habibicafeteria

The latest newcomer to Veracruz’s growing and diversifying coffee scene, Habibi opened its doors earlier this summer and added something completely fresh and rare to the port city’s culinary sphere: a Turkish-inspired café. Found in the ever-trendy Reforma neighborhood, the decor here is a bit over the top and kitschy, but the spirit of the coffee and food is unique and notable. Order a Turkish coffee (which is brewed in hot sand) and, if you’re hungering or have a sweet tooth, add a side of gold-dusted dessert — or grab a loaded shawarma de pollo — and stay for the fun of it all. Pro tip: don’t forget the plátano macho-stuffed kibbeh.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Aquí si volvemos (@aquisivolvemos)

The tropical abundance of Veracruz’s ingredients reigns supreme at DeLirio. Take your pick of orange espressos, pineapple cold brews, maracuya cheesecakes, watermelon agua frescas, chilled cucumbers and lime frappes, and so much more. Despite its colorful vibrancy on the menu, it retains an understated interior style: An elegant, minimalist architecture highlighted by its mid-century-inspired curved walls and wicker chairs — all working in harmony to accentuate this chic café in (you guessed it) Colonia Reforma.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020) and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: MND launches new series on personal finance
World.content:
The team at Mexico News Daily is always trying to think of new content ideas to help better educate and inform our readers about Mexico. A few recent examples include our Expat Safety Perceptions Index, the MND Mexico Healthcare Survey, and the Sheinbaum, Mexico Economy, and Peso Indexes.

As we have been working on these content ideas over the past few months, we have received feedback from readers on other ideas, and we have identified some additional gaps as well. One of them is to create an index that focuses more on Mexico’s social progress (or lack of) versus more economically focused indicators. We are actively working on that one — stay tuned!

Another big gap we identified was regarding the whole issue of money and personal finance in Mexico. It occurred to us that there is often a real gap in knowledge when it comes to money in Mexico. Many people who are extremely sophisticated financially in their home country oftentimes don’t even have a bank account in Mexico. Others that I have met have little more than a local basic checking account with a debit card. Still others lose significant amounts of money on currency conversion.

The light bulb really went off when we were reviewing the results of the Expat Safety Perceptions Index. The data of our survey showed us that most expats/foreigners have not had personal safety issues and in fact, for the most part, feel very safe in Mexico. From a personal safety perspective, most feel pretty good. But that got us thinking and asking questions like:

1. What financial issues have you had in Mexico?

2. What are the financial risks the immigrants face here?

3. What are common mistakes that immigrants make with money here?

4. How many MND readers have been victims of a financial crime in Mexico?

5. What can you do to protect your finances in Mexico?

We believe that this is an extremely important topic and there is much to be learned and applied. As a result, Mexico News Daily will be going “all in” on this topic. We will start with a survey that we will be asking thousands of expats in Mexico to take. The results of this survey will be shared with our readers and will also help guide and define the topics of a new weekly series of “Mexico and My Money,” beginning next week. In this series, we will be covering everything from common mistakes made to best practices for protecting and growing your money in Mexico. We will cover topics like banking, exchanging money, rental income, investing, and dealing with contractors and local service providers.

Our goal is neither to scare you nor lead you to a false sense of security, but rather to provide you with the information, best practices and lessons learned of others to help you best manage your money in Mexico. Stay tuned, I am certain that we are all going to learn a lot from this survey and series.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: An award-winning bakery launches a definitive ‘map’ of Mexico’s abundant bread types
World.content:
Building on Mexico News Daily’s history of Mexican bread, published earlier this year, two Mexican bakers have created a new “map” that charts the vast, often overlooked world of Mexican breads — from conchas and bolillos to coyotas, pan de muerto and rosca de Reyes.

The Primer Mapa del Pan Mexicano — or First Map of Mexican Bread — is a research project by siblings Ariana and Julio González, the founding bakers at 13-year-old Buñuelo in Naucalpan, State of México.

Instead of sorting breads by state or region, the map tracks their baking lineage: dough, technique and tradition.

That framework shows how one preparation style can develop into breads with markedly different shapes, textures and uses, with seemingly unrelated pieces sharing production methods or customs.

The map includes sweet breads, or pan dulce, savory staples and festive breads such as pan de muerto for Día de Muertos and rosca de Reyes for Three Kings Day.

The savory family includes bolillo, telera, pambazo, cemita and hojaldra, breads commonly used in tortas and other Mexican sandwiches.

Other families include bizcocho — sweet, cake-like breads including conchas, nubes and pelones — and the cookie family, which includes cochinitos de piloncillo, coricos and coyotas, the last being Sonoran pastries typically filled with piloncillo.

Other breads in the festive category include pan de pulque, pan de yema and a specialty bread sold at festivals and patron saint celebrations in Puebla and Tlaxcala called pan de fiesta or pan de feria.

The González siblings — recently named Bakers of the Year by the Mexico Gastronomic Guide — developed the project through years of fieldwork at traditional and contemporary bakeries. Designer Marcela Morales turned the research into a reference piece.

The total number of Mexican breads remains an elusive proposition. Estimates often put the figure above 1,000 varieties, but the map is not presented as a census. Its 52 selections are representative samples meant to illuminate a larger and still-changing baking heritage.

“This map is not intended to be a definitive catalog of Mexican breadmaking, but rather an invitation to see it from a different perspective,” Julio González said, “We want people to understand that behind each piece there are techniques, traditions, and baking families that are all part of the same heritage.”

The map arrives after a period of renewed attention to Mexican breadmaking.

In late 2025, a British baker based in Mexico City voiced a blunt opinion about Mexican bread culture (or, in his opinion, lack thereof) and received widespread backlash, including a Mexico News Daily piece noting, “You’re free to dislike bolillos … Just don’t use cultural superiority as a seasoning.”

Then earlier this year, Panadería Rosetta in Mexico City was named one of the world’s 10 best pastry makers by La Liste, a prestigious Paris‑based global dining guide.

For now, the single-sheet map is being sold for 135 pesos (US $7.88) at Buñuelo, Av. Alcanfores 44-2 in Naucalpan. See the bakery’s Instagram for more details, including a planned digital version.

With reports from Food & Wine en Español and El Universal

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 8, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Editor’s note, 9 August 2026. This listing named two events that were not taking place on Saturday 8 August. Danny Krivit played Heavy House on Thursday 6 August, the opening night of the club’s anniversary run; Saturday’s bill was Malu b2b Bauhouse, Gui Paiola b2b MOA Records and Beto Chuquer. The SP2B festival at Ibirapuera runs from 9 to 16 August and had not begun; Criolo plays on 15 August and BaianaSystem on 16 August. We apologise to readers who went out on the strength of these entries.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Blue Note São Paulo A verified landmark from our venue database – jazz shows tonight – a reliable Paulista standby.

Tonight at a Glance —Heavy House (Pinheiros) House music marathon from 4 pm till late. Malu b2b Bauhouse, Gui Paiola b2b MOA Records and Beto Chuquer on the decks. Mixed crowd of music heads, expats and night owls. —Alessandra Leão at Masp vão livre (Paulista) Free open-air show reimagining Alceu Valença’s Nordeste classics. Perfect early-evening culture stop before heading out. Paulista Avenue energy. —D-Edge (Barra Funda) Saturday electronic night at SP’s most famous club. World-class soundsystem, international DJs, and a terrace for sunrise. Always a safe bet. —Clash Club (Barra Funda) Saturday club night with indie, rock and electronic rooms. Grungy-cool crowd, near D-Edge for a two-club crawl. —Bourbon Street Music Club (Moema) Live music Saturday in an intimate setting. Jazz, blues or MPB depending on the night. Older, sophisticated crowd. Great for date night.

Saturday night in São Paulo belongs to Heavy House. The Pinheiros staple continues its eight-year anniversary run with a stacked local lineup from 4 pm to 4 am. New York house don Danny Krivit played the opening night on Thursday. For an early cultural hit, catch Alessandra Leão’s free tribute to Alceu Valença under the Masp vão, then dive into the Barra Funda club strip.

Tonight across São Paulo. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Alessandra Leão canta Alceu Valença – free show at Masp vão livre — at Masp (vão livre), late afternoon, typically between 4 pm and 6 pm. Beautiful open-air set reimagining the Pernambuco surrealist’s songbook. Part of the Música no Masp series. Grab a coconut water from a street vendor and soak in the Paulista Avenue scene.

SP2B Festival at Ibirapuera opens tomorrow – free outdoor shows from 9 to 16 August — at Auditório Ibirapuera (área externa), afternoon/evening (festival runs all day). Over 40 free shows across the Ibirapuera park area as part of the São Paulo Beyond Business festival, which runs from 9 to 16 August. Criolo plays on 15 August, BaianaSystem on 16 August.

‘A Odisseia’ – Christopher Nolan’s epic screens at cinemas — at various cinemas (check Itaú, Cinemark, Reserva Cultural), evening sessions. A quiet alternative to the club scene. Nolan’s adaptation of Homer is drawing crowds and debate. Catch an evening screening if you need a breather after a heavy Friday.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Start at Masp vão (around 4 pm): Alessandra Leão’s free show. Grab a pastel and caldo de cana from a street cart on Paulista.

Move to Ibirapuera: the park is gorgeous at golden hour, though the SP2B stages open only tomorrow.

Dinner in Pinheiros: Sardosa Bar on Vila Madalena’s edge does excellent caipira food. Or grab a bite near Heavy House on Rua Benjamim Egas.

Heavy House (10 pm onward): hit the dancefloor for the anniversary lineup. The party runs to 4 am.

After-hours crawl: D-Edge and Clash Club are a 10-minute Uber from Heavy House in Barra Funda. Both go past sunrise.

Scenes & Sounds

House & Electronic — São Paulo’s electronic scene rivals Berlin and London. Heavy House anchors the Pinheiros underground, while D-Edge in Barra Funda draws international headliners with a Funktion-One soundsystem. Where: Heavy House (Pinheiros), D-Edge (Barra Funda), Clash Club (Barra Funda)

Samba & Pagode — Saturday samba is a religion here. Live roda de samba spills from bars in Vila Madalena and Lapa. Expect cold beer, cachaça shots and singalong choruses. Where: Bar Mangueira, Ó do Borogodó (Pinheiros), Sesc Pompeia (event-based)

MPB & Jazz — Intimate listening rooms with couvert artístico (a per-person music charge). World-class musicians play for attentive crowds over dinner and drinks. Where: Casa de Francisca (Sé/Centro), Bourbon Street Music Club (Moema), Blue Note (Paulista)

Forró — Forró parties draw a mixed crowd of Brazilians and curious foreigners. Live trios with accordion, zabumba and triangle. Lessons early in the night if you ask. Where: Canto da Ema (Pinheiros), events at Sesc Pompeia

Funk & Baile — São Paulo baile funk is grittier and faster than Rio’s. Sound systems shake the walls of clubs and street parties in the city’s outer neighbourhoods. Go with a local guide. Where: Clash Club (special nights), street parties in Capão Redondo or Brasilândia (guided only)

Indie & Rock — Saturday nights at Clash Club orbit guitar bands, Britpop and indie dancefloors. Galeria do Rock on Avenida São João is a daytime pilgrimage for vinyl and band tees. Where: Clash Club (Barra Funda), Galeria do Rock (República/Centro)

Pick Your Night

Dance till sunrise: Heavy House 8th Anniversary, then D-Edge. Start at 11 pm at Heavy House for the anniversary lineup. Move to D-Edge around 3 am as the terrace sun comes up.

Date night: Bourbon Street Music Club in Moema. Intimate live jazz or MPB, tableside service, great cocktails. Book a table ahead. Then a late drink at a nearby Moema bar.

Solo and safe: Alessandra Leão at Masp vão (free, open-air, easy to slip in and out). Then a solo dinner at a Pinheiros boteco. São Paulo is forgiving for solo diners at bar counters.

Meet locals: Any roda de samba in Vila Madalena on a Saturday afternoon. Tables are communal. Share a bucket of beer and you’ll be singing the chorus by the third song.

Chill and conversation: Casa de Francisca in Sé. An elegant early-20th-century palacete turned listening room. Buy a couvert online, order a sparkling wine, and let the music carry the evening.

Where to Go

Heavy House — Pinheiros Eight-year-old house music institution with a loyal crowd of music purists, expats and nightlife workers. The Saturday anniversary bash is the weekend’s centrepiece. Tonight: 8th Anniversary, night three: Malu b2b Bauhouse, Gui Paiola b2b MOA Records, Beto Chuquer. Danny Krivit played the Thursday opening. 4 pm–4 am. Best time: Friday and Saturday nights for top local and international DJs. Arrive after 11 pm for peak energy. Wednesday and Thursday are lower-key with resident selectors. Cost: Entry R$40–R$100 depending on lineup, about US$8–20. Drinks from R$20 (beer) to R$45 (cocktails), roughly US$4–9. Cash and card accepted. Address: Rua Benjamim Egas, 297, Pinheiros Instagram: @heavyhousesp Website: baressp.com.br/shows/heavy-house-celebra-oito-anos-com-show-inedito-de-danny-krivit- Getting there: Metro Fradique Coutinho (Line 4 Yellow) is a 12-minute walk. Uber recommended at night — set pickup to the Benjamim Egas corner. Good to know: Book ahead via the venue’s ticketing link for big nights. No strict door policy but smart-casual helps. Bring ID.

Masp — Paulista São Paulo’s iconic art museum with a famous open-air void underneath. Free weekend music series draws a democratic crowd of art students, families and tourists. Tonight: Alessandra Leão sings Alceu Valença as part of the Música no Masp series. Free, open-air, late afternoon. Best time: Weekend afternoons for the vão livre programme. Tuesday is free museum entry all day. Arrive early for a good spot on the steps. Cost: Free entry for vão livre events. Museum entry R$85, about US$17, and free on Tuesdays. Street vendors sell coconut water and snacks from R$5, about US$1. Address: Av. Paulista 1578, Bela Vista Phone: +55 11 3149-5959 Instagram: @maspmuseu Website: masp.org.br Getting there: Metro Trianon-Masp (Line 2 Green) exits directly onto Paulista Avenue. Buses run along Paulista. Uber drops at the side entrance. Good to know: No booking needed for vão events. Arrive 30 minutes early for a decent spot.

D-Edge — Barra Funda São Paulo’s most internationally famous club. Impeccable Funktion-One sound, a light show that rivals Berlin, and a terrace where you watch the sunrise over the city. Tonight: Saturday electronic night — check @dedgeclub for the exact lineup. Typically house or techno. Best time: Saturday for the biggest lineups. Arrive between midnight and 1 am. The terrace peaks around 4 am. Cost: Entry R$80–R$150, about US$16–30. Comanda card system — pay at the end. Drinks R$25–R$40, about US$5–8. Cash and card. Address: Al. Olga 170, Barra Funda Phone: +55 11 3666-9399 Instagram: @dedgeclub Website: d-edge.com.br Getting there: Metro Marechal Deodoro (Line 3 Red) is a 15-minute walk. Uber strongly recommended at night. The street is quiet and industrial — the club’s black facade is the landmark. Good to know: Buy tickets online via the website. Door policy is relaxed but no flip-flops or football jerseys. Comanda card: DO NOT LOSE IT — replacement fees are steep.

Clash Club — Barra Funda Grungy-cool two-floor club a block from D-Edge. Indie rock, electro and occasional hip-hop rooms. Younger, less-polished crowd than D-Edge. Tonight: Saturday club night — check @clashclubsp for room splits. Best time: Saturday nights. Arrive after midnight. Catch a band on the ground floor then move to the DJ room upstairs. Cost: Entry R$30–R$70, about US$6–14. Drinks from R$15 (US$3) for a beer. Cash and card accepted. Address: Rua Barra Funda 969, Barra Funda Instagram: @clashclubsp Website: clashclub.com.br Getting there: Same as D-Edge: Metro Marechal Deodoro (15 min walk) or Uber. Pair both clubs in one night. Good to know: Tickets at the door usually fine. No strict dress code. Bring ID.

Bourbon Street Music Club — Moema Intimate jazz and MPB listening room inspired by New Orleans clubs. Great acoustics, candlelit tables, and a sophisticated over-30s crowd. Perfect for date night. Tonight: Saturday live music (lineup varies weekly — check Instagram @bourbonstreetbrasil for tonight’s act). Best time: Friday and Saturday for live music. Arrive by 9 pm for dinner before the show starts around 10 pm. Shows typically run two sets. Cost: Couvert artístico R$40–R$80 (about US$8–16). Main courses R$60–R$120 (US$12–24). Cocktails R$35–R$45 (US$7–9). Credit and debit cards accepted. Address: Rua dos Chanes 127, Moema Phone: +55 11 2309-4703 Instagram: @bourbonstreetbrasil Website: bourbonstreet.com.br Getting there: Metro Eucaliptos (Line 5 Lilac) is a 10-minute walk. Uber is easier — Moema is safe and well-lit. Good to know: Strongly recommended to book a table via the website. Dress smart-casual. No shorts or flip-flops after dark.

Casa de Francisca — Sé/Centro A jewel-box listening room inside the Palacete Teresa. Intimate acoustic sets of MPB, samba and instrumental music. The bar serves excellent sparkling wine and small plates. Tonight: Saturday show — check @casadefrancisca for the bill and buy couvert online. Best time: Thursday, Friday and Saturday shows. Arrive at 8 pm for a good seat. The 1920s mansion is worth seeing in daylight. Cost: Couvert artístico R$50–R$80 (about US$10–16). Drinks R$25–R$45 (US$5–9). Small plates from R$35 (US$7). Cash and card accepted. Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiuva 22, Sé (Palacete Teresa) Phone: +55 11 3101-4159 Instagram: @casadefrancisca Website: casadefrancisca.com.br Getting there: Metro Sé (Lines 1 Blue and 3 Red) is a 5-minute walk. The Sé area can feel sketchy after dark — take an Uber straight to the door. Good to know: Buy couvert online ahead of time. The house seats only 80 people, and Saturday sells out. No strict dress code.

Auditório Ibirapuera (área externa) — Parque Ibirapuera The outdoor stage at Ibirapuera Park hosts the SP2B festival with 40+ free shows from 9 to 16 August. Criolo plays 15 August, BaianaSystem 16 August. Picnic blankets and park vibes. Tonight: Nothing here tonight: SP2B opens on 9 August. Free once it starts, afternoon and evening. Best time: Arrive early afternoon to claim a patch of grass. Shows run all day. Food trucks on site. The park closes at midnight. Cost: Free entry. Food truck meals R$25–R$45, about US$5–9. Drinks R$10–R$20 from vendors, about US$2–4. Address: Av. Pedro Álvares Cabral, s/n, portão 3, Parque Ibirapuera Getting there: Metro AACD-Servidor (Line 5 Lilac) is closest. Buses along Avenida Pedro Álvares Cabral. Uber drops at portão 3. Walk through the park to the stage area. Good to know: No booking. Free entry. Arrive early for the best acts. Bring sunscreen, water and a jacket for when the temperature drops.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Pinheiros: The gastronomic and bohemian heart of the west zone. Restaurant-heavy during the day, bar-heavy at night. Rua dos Pinheiros and Rua Benjamim Egas are the main strips.

Barra Funda: Former industrial zone turned clubland. D-Edge and Clash Club anchor a gritty, serious-nightlife strip. Best reached by Uber after dark.

Paulista: The city’s grand avenue. Museums by day, hotel bars and Blue Note by night. Masp’s vão livre is São Paulo’s democratic living room.

Vila Madalena: Street-party energy on weekends. Botecos and samba bars overflow onto the pavements. Younger, student-leaning crowd. Great for bar-hopping on foot.

Moema: Leafy, affluent and quieter. Bourbon Street is the nightlife anchor. Better for dinner-and-a-show dates than wild partying.

Sé/Centro: Historic downtown with pockets of magic like Casa de Francisca. Beautiful architecture, can feel edgy after dark. Go point-to-point via Uber.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Heavy House (Pinheiros) — Mixed, LGBTQ-friendly crowd. The house music scene in SP is proudly inclusive. Saturday’s anniversary will be a safe, diverse dancefloor.

D-Edge (Barra Funda) — Legendary LGBTQ-friendly club. No strict door, no pretension — just good music and a famously open vibe. Saturday terrace is always a friendly mix.

Rua Augusta and around Praça Roosevelt — São Paulo’s unofficial queer nightlife corridor. Several small clubs and bars within walking distance. Explore with caution late at night and stick to well-lit streets.

Money & How Paying Works Comanda card system: clubs like D-Edge give you a card at entry. All drinks are charged to it, and you settle the bill at the exit. Do not lose it — replacement fees can be R$50–R$100, about US$10–20. Couvert artístico: a per-person music charge added to your bill at live music venues like Bourbon Street and Casa de Francisca. Typically R$40–R$80, about US$8–16. It’s not optional and supports the musicians. Cash vs card: São Paulo is card-friendly nearly everywhere, including street vendors with Pix instant payments. But keep R$50–R$100, about US$10–20, in small notes for door covers at informal samba bars. Tipping: 10% service charge is usually included on the bill (look for ‘serviço’ or ‘10%’). You can tip extra for exceptional service, but it’s not expected. Bartenders appreciate a R$5–R$10 note, about US$1–2, per round.

Getting Home Safe

Metro closes at midnight on Saturday (technically midnight Sunday morning). Last trains leave termini around midnight. Do not rely on the metro to get home from a late night.

Uber and 99 (local rival) are reliable and affordable. A trip from Barra Funda to Pinheiros costs about R$25–R$35, roughly US$5–7. From Barra Funda to Jardins or Paulista is R$30–R$45, about US$6–9. Late-night surge after 2 am adds 20–50%.

Safe pickup: at club exits, request your ride while still inside, wait until you see the car’s plate, and walk out directly to it. Do not stand on the kerb waving your phone at 4 am.

São Paulo is a big, watchful city. Phone snatching is the most common risk — when you step outside a club to check your ride, cup the phone in both hands and be quick.

Stick to main streets and well-lit areas when walking between nearby venues. Pinheiros and Vila Madalena are walkable bar-hopping neighbourhoods. Barra Funda’s club strip is fine point-to-point but do not wander onto empty side streets.

More: Brazil news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time should I go out on a Saturday?

Dinner and drinks from 8 pm, live music from 9–10 pm, clubs from midnight, peak dancefloor 1–3 am, sunrise terrace 4 am. São Paulo runs late — showing up at 11 pm is perfectly normal.

Do I need to speak Portuguese to enjoy the nightlife?

For clubs and electronic music, no — music is the universal language. For samba bars and MPB listening rooms, a few phrases help enormously. ‘Uma cerveja, por favor’ (a beer, please) and ‘obrigado/a’ (thank you) go a long way.

What’s the dress code in São Paulo clubs?

Smart-casual rules most places. No flip-flops, no football jerseys, no shorts at upscale venues like Bourbon Street. Sneakers and a button-down or black tee will get you in anywhere. Bring a light layer — air conditioning is aggressive.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 8, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Editor’s note, 9 August 2026. The cinema listing said screenings ran daily at Cinesystem Belas Artes until 25 August. That venue’s run was 3 to 5 August; the festival continues elsewhere until 25 August. There was no screening there on the evening of 8 August.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Carioca Da Gema A verified landmark from our venue database – live samba/MPB tonight – a reliable Lapa standby.

Tonight at a Glance —Carioca da Gema The most reliable Saturday samba in Lapa. Live MPB and samba, a mixed crowd of locals and visitors, best from 10 pm. —Rio Scenarium A three-floor antique wonderland with live samba and forró bands on Saturday nights. Go early to beat the queue. —V Mostra de Cinema China-Brasil Free screenings of Chinese and Brazilian films at festival venues across the city; the Cinesystem Belas Artes run ended on 5 August. —Pedra do Sal The historic birthplace of samba runs its roda on Monday, not Saturday; plan ahead for next week. —Trapiche Gamboa A polished samba and forró spot in Gamboa. A good Plan B if Lapa feels too chaotic.

Tonight is an unusually quiet Saturday for headline events in Rio, with no major listed parties or shows on this date. The real action is in the city’s trusted weekly samba standbys in Lapa and a free China-Brazil film festival in Botafogo.

Tonight across Rio de Janeiro. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm up 8 pm: Grab a caipirinha at a boteco on Av. Mem de Sá in Lapa and watch the street party come alive.

Prime time 10 pm: Hit Carioca da Gema or Rio Scenarium for live samba. Expect a couvert artístico of R$30-50, about US$6-10, at the door.

Late night 1 am: Follow the crowd to the post-samba street scene under the Arcos da Lapa for grilled street food and cold beer.

Alternative 7 pm: See a free Chinese film at Cinesystem Belas Artes in Botafogo, then stroll to a bar on Rua Nelson Mandela.

Sunday recovery: Bip Bip in Copacabana hosts its intimate roda de samba from 7 pm. Get there by 6 pm for a table.

Midweek planner: Pedra do Sal’s famous street roda is a Monday night, from 7 pm, with a smaller Friday session run by a different collective. Never Saturday. Bookmark it for later.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba — The heartbeat of Saturday night in Rio. Carioca da Gema and Rio Scenarium deliver live bands and a buzzing, cross-generational crowd in Lapa. Trapiche Gamboa offers a more polished alternative. Where: Av. Mem de Sá and Rua do Lavradio, Lapa; Rua Sacadura Cabral, Gamboa

MPB — Música Popular Brasileira blends with samba at Carioca da Gema. Expect classics from Jobim to contemporary artists in an intimate, air-conditioned setting. Where: Carioca da Gema, Av. Mem de Sá 79, Lapa

Forró — The accordion-driven dance from the Northeast is alive at Rio Scenarium and Trapiche Gamboa. Both venues mix forró sets with samba on Saturday nights. Where: Rio Scenarium, Rua do Lavradio 20, Centro; Trapiche Gamboa, Rua Sacadura Cabral 155, Gamboa

Electronic — Electronic music is not Lapa’s Saturday strength, and nothing is promoted tonight. Teatro Odisseia posts late additions and pop-up parties to Instagram on the day. Where: Teatro Odisseia, Av. Mem de Sá 66, Lapa

Cinema — The free V Mostra de Cinema China-Brasil runs until 25 August at schools and cultural centres, blending Jackie Chan action with Brazilian music documentaries; its Cinesystem Belas Artes run ended on 5 August. A cultured, quiet alternative to the Lapa crush. Where: Cinesystem Belas Artes, Praia de Botafogo 316, Botafogo

Pick Your Night

Dance till sunrise: Start at Rio Scenarium for three floors of live samba and forró, then spill out onto the Lapa streets where the party keeps going until dawn.

Date night: Trapiche Gamboa in Gamboa. A handsome, renovated warehouse with a mezzanine, good acoustics, and a slightly older crowd.

Solo and safe: Carioca da Gema in Lapa. The cosy, air-conditioned room is welcoming and easy to navigate alone. Sit at the bar, order a cold beer, and the music does the rest.

Meet locals: The street party under the Arcos da Lapa after midnight. Grab a R$10 caipirinha, about US$2, from a cart, lean against a wall, and you’ll be chatting to cariocas within minutes.

Chill and conversation: Bip Bip in Copacabana. Though its roda de samba is Sunday, tonight it serves as a low-key boteco for a quiet beer and conversation before the bigger night.

Where to Go

Carioca da Gema — Lapa The most consistent live samba house in Lapa. An intimate, air-conditioned room with a mezzanine, drawing a mix of tourists, expats and samba-loving locals. Tonight: Live samba/MPB from 10 pm. A reliable Saturday weekly standby. Best time: Saturdays from 10 pm. Arrive by 9:30 pm to get a table. Bands rotate between classic samba and MPB. Cost: Couvert artístico R$30-50 (about US$6-10). Beer R$12-15 (US$2.40-3). Cash and cards accepted. Address: Av. Mem de Sa 79, Lapa Instagram: @cariocadagema Getting there: Rideshare to Av. Mem de Sá. Cinelândia metro is a 12-minute walk. Do not walk from the metro alone late at night; take 99 or Uber door to door. Good to know: No booking for small groups. Arrive early. Smart-casual; no shorts for men on Saturdays.

Rio Scenarium — Centro/Lapa A three-storey antique-filled wonderland and Rio’s most famous nightlife address. Live samba and forró bands, a restaurant, and a crowd that spans every continent. Tonight: Live samba/forró bands from 8 pm. A reliable Saturday weekly standby. Best time: Saturdays from 9 pm. The line builds by 8 pm. Go early, eat a feijoada, and claim a spot near the stage. Cost: Entry R$40-70 (about US$8-14). Main dishes R$60-90 (US$12-18). Beer R$14 (US$2.75). All cards accepted. Comanda card system at the door. Address: Rua do Lavradio 20, Centro Phone: +55 21 3147-9000 Instagram: @rioscenarium Website: www.rioscenarium.com.br Getting there: Rideshare to the door. Cinelândia metro is a 10-minute walk; take a taxi or Uber after 10 pm. Good to know: Book online for a table in the restaurant. Street queue for the bar. Dress smart-casual; no flip-flops.

Trapiche Gamboa — Gamboa A beautifully restored port warehouse with exposed brick, a mezzanine balcony, and top-tier samba and forró bands. A more refined alternative to the Lapa crush, popular with an over-30 crowd and couples. Tonight: Live samba/forró from 9 pm. A reliable Saturday weekly standby. Best time: Saturdays from 9:30 pm. The mezzanine has the best sightlines. Bands lean towards classic samba. Cost: Entry R$30-50 (about US$6-10). Cocktails R$25-35 (US$5-7). Cards accepted. Comanda system. Address: Rua Sacadura Cabral 155, Gamboa Instagram: @trapichegamboa Getting there: Rideshare only. The port area is quiet at night. Instruct your driver to collect you directly at the door. Good to know: Reserve a table for the mezzanine via Instagram DM. Mixed dress code.

Bip Bip — Copacabana A tiny, legendary boteco that feels like a living museum of samba. No stage, no microphone, no set list. The Sunday roda de samba is a sacred carioca ritual, but tonight it’s a quiet spot for a cold beer. Tonight: No live music tonight. Open as a neighbourhood boteco for a quiet beer. Best time: Sunday roda de samba from 7 pm. Tuesday choro. Arrive by 6 pm on Sunday for a pavement table. Cost: Beer R$10-12, about US$2-2.40. Cash only. No entry fee except on music nights (voluntary contribution). Address: Rua Almirante Goncalves 50, Copacabana Instagram: @bipbipbar Getting there: Cantagalo metro station, then a 5-minute walk. Safe, well-lit area. Rideshare easy. Good to know: No bookings. Just show up. Very casual.

Pedra do Sal — Saúde The sacred birthplace of samba, an open-air street party around a large rock in the historic port district. A mix of old-guard sambistas, young locals and clued-in visitors. Tonight: No roda tonight. The main roda is Monday, with a smaller Friday session. Empty on Saturday. Best time: Monday from 7 pm to midnight for the main roda. Arrive by 6:30 pm for a place on the stone. Cost: Free entry. Street vendors sell beer at R$8-10 (about US$1.60-2) and caipirinhas at R$15 (US$3). Cash preferred. Address: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde Getting there: Rideshare or VLT to Parada dos Museus. Do not walk from surrounding streets late at night. Good to know: No bookings. Outdoor public space.

Cinesystem Belas Artes — Botafogo A classic modern cinema in Botafogo’s Praia Shopping, hosting the free V Mostra de Cinema China-Brasil with 14 films throughout August. Tonight: No screening here tonight – the Cinesystem Belas Artes run ended on 5 August. The festival continues at other venues until 25 August. Best time: The Cinesystem Belas Artes run was 3 to 5 August; the festival continues until 25 August at schools and cultural centres. All free. Cost: Free entry. Check schedule at the box office or observatoriodachina.org. Address: Praia de Botafogo 316, Botafogo Getting there: Botafogo metro, then a 5-minute walk. Area is busy and well-lit. Rideshare to Praia Shopping. Good to know: Arrive early as screenings are free and seats fill up.

Circo Voador — Lapa Rio’s historic open-air venue under the Arcos da Lapa, hosting everything from Brazilian rock to international DJs. Always worth checking the calendar. Tonight: Nothing on the bill tonight; the venue adds late shows to its website. Best time: Event-based schedule. Doors usually open at 9 pm. Check circoavoador.com.br for upcoming shows. Cost: Varies by event, typically R$60-120, about US$12-24. Cards accepted. Online ticket purchase recommended. Address: Rua dos Arcos s/n, Lapa Instagram: @circoavoador Website: www.circoavoador.com.br Getting there: Rideshare to the door. Cinelândia metro is a 10-minute walk; take a taxi back. Good to know: Buy tickets online in advance. Events often sell out.

Fundição Progresso — Lapa A vast, multi-room cultural centre and concert hall in a former foundry. Hosts major shows, festivals, and pop-up events. Tonight: Nothing on the bill tonight; late additions go out on its social channels. Best time: Event-based. Check fundicaoprogresso.com.br. Usually 10 pm start for music. Cost: Varies by event. Bar inside accepts cards. Cash for street vendors outside. Address: Rua dos Arcos 24, Lapa Instagram: @fundicaoprogresso Website: www.fundicaoprogresso.com.br Getting there: Rideshare. Same advice as Circo Voador. Do not wander the side streets. Good to know: Online tickets recommended.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Lapa: The roaring heart of Rio’s Saturday night, where the streets fill with samba, street food and a cross-section of the entire city.

Botafogo: A young, middle-class neighbourhood with a thriving cinema scene, craft beer bars on Rua Nelson Mandela, and a less touristy feel.

Gamboa: A regenerated port district with polished samba venues and a more local, over-30 crowd seeking quality over chaos.

Copacabana: The classic beach neighbourhood, quieter at night beyond the Avenida Atlântica kiosks, with a handful of cherished local institutions.

Saúde: The historic port, home to Pedra do Sal and a daytime museum circuit, quietens down on Saturdays but is essential for Monday-night samba.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Teatro Odisseia — A Lapa venue with an eclectic programme that often includes LGBTQ-friendly parties and drag nights. Check their Instagram for tonight’s lineup, though nothing is confirmed for this date.

Rua Farme de Amoedo, Ipanema — Rio’s most famous gay-friendly beach by day, the surrounding bars and small clubs in Ipanema are a reliable fallback for a mixed, welcoming crowd on Saturday nights.

Money & How Paying Works Comanda card: At Rio Scenarium and Trapiche Gamboa, you get a card at the door. All drinks and food are charged to it. Pay the total at the exit cashier. Do not lose the card; there is a steep fee. Couvert artístico: A per-person music charge of R$30-50, about US$6-10, at live samba venues, added to your bill or charged at the door. Not optional; it pays the musicians. Cash vs card: Lapa street vendors and small botecos like Bip Bip are cash-only. Larger venues accept all cards. Carry R$200, about US$40, in cash as a safety net. Tipping: Not obligatory but 10% is standard for table service in bars and restaurants. Bartenders appreciate a couple of reais per round.

Getting Home Safe

Metro closes at midnight on Saturday. Do not rely on it to get home after a late night. Plan for rideshare.

Use 99 or Uber. Choose ‘Comfort’ or ‘Black’ for newer cars with confirmed drivers. Wait inside the venue or in its doorway until the car arrives and you verify the plate.

Avoid hailing street taxis after midnight in Lapa. They often refuse to use the meter and overcharge. Stick to app-based rides.

Stay on the main streets in Lapa. The action is on Av. Mem de Sá, Rua do Lavradio, and around the Arcos. Side streets, especially heading towards the Santa Teresa hill, are poorly lit and should be avoided. Keep your phone in your front pocket when in dense crowds, and do not leave bags hanging on chair backs.

In Gamboa and Saúde, the surroundings are quiet. Use rideshare door to door, even for short distances. Street lighting is patchy and there are few people around outside venue hours.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time does the samba start in Lapa?

Live bands at Carioca da Gema and Rio Scenarium start around 9-10 pm. The street scene picks up after 11 pm and runs past 3 am.

Do I need to buy tickets in advance?

For the free V Mostra de Cinema, just show up early. For samba venues, you pay at the door. Only Circo Voador or Fundição Progresso shows require advance online tickets.

Is it safe to walk back to my hotel from Lapa?

No. Use a rideshare app even if your hotel is in nearby Santa Teresa, Gloria or Centro. The streets empty quickly and lighting is poor.

Sources: observatoriodachina.org, extra.globo.com, contextoexato.com.br

World.title: Colombia’s New President Says the Wealth Tax Will Go — What That Means if You Live There
World.content:
Colombia · Taxes

Key Facts The pledge. President Abelardo De La Espriella said in his inaugural address on 7 August that the wealth tax will be abolished: “we must stop punishing those who invest and generate wealth.”

President Abelardo De La Espriella said in his inaugural address on 7 August that the wealth tax will be abolished: “we must stop punishing those who invest and generate wealth.” Not law. It is an announcement. Abolition requires a structural tax reform passed by Congress, and no bill has been filed.

It is an announcement. Abolition requires a structural tax reform passed by Congress, and no bill has been filed. Also announced. A decree freezing public spending, the recovery of Ecopetrol as a priority, and the re-authorisation of fracking.

A decree freezing public spending, the recovery of Ecopetrol as a priority, and the re-authorisation of fracking. Why it matters to you. The impuesto al patrimonio is the levy that reaches foreign tax residents in Colombia on their worldwide assets above the threshold.

The impuesto al patrimonio is the levy that reaches foreign tax residents in Colombia on their worldwide assets above the threshold. The setting. He gave the address from the Cantón Militar Pichincha, a military garrison, rather than from Bogotá.

Colombia’s new president says the wealth tax will go. It is the levy that reaches foreign residents’ worldwide assets — and it is an announcement, not a law.

The Colombia wealth tax is the first thing the new government named. In his inaugural address on Friday, Abelardo De La Espriella said the impuesto al patrimonio would be abolished as the centrepiece of a structural tax reform, because the country “must stop punishing those who invest and generate wealth”. For foreigners weighing Colombian tax residency, no other line in that speech matters as much — and none is further from being law.

Colombia’s New President Says the Wealth Tax Will Go — What That Means if You Live There. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Colombia wealth tax pledge actually is

De La Espriella took the oath at 3 p.m. on Friday at the Universidad Santiago de Cali, then delivered his first address from a military garrison. The economic content was the part that matters to anyone with assets in Colombia. He named a structural tax reform, and named its headline measure: the wealth tax goes.

Alongside it he said he would sign a decree freezing public spending “in the coming hours”, called the recovery of Ecopetrol an absolute priority, and confirmed that Colombia will re-authorise fracking under what he called responsible and sustainable technical standards.

Be clear about what this is. Abolishing the impuesto al patrimonio is not something a president can decree. It requires a tax reform bill through both chambers of Congress, and the previous government’s own tax reform died there in July. No bill has been filed. What exists today is a stated intention from a president on his first day.

Why the wealth tax matters to foreign residents specifically

Colombia taxes its tax residents on worldwide income and worldwide assets. You become a tax resident by spending more than 183 days in the country across any rolling 365-day period, and the clock does not reset at the calendar year.

For most foreigners the income side is manageable, because Colombia gives credit for tax paid abroad. The asset side is the one that catches people out. The wealth tax applies to net worth above the threshold, wherever in the world that wealth sits — a house in Europe, a pension pot, a brokerage account. For a retiree or a remote worker with accumulated savings, it can turn a comfortable cost-of-living arbitrage into an expensive one.

That is why this announcement is worth more attention than a typical tax headline. It is not a rate tweak. It is the specific provision that most often decides whether someone lets the 183-day clock run out or leaves before it does.

Colombians have already had one scare on this. In December the outgoing government used emergency powers to cut the entry threshold from 72,000 UVT to 40,000 UVT, a change that would have brought the total number of people liable to around 105,000, including plenty of foreign residents who had never expected to file. The Constitutional Court suspended the decree in January and struck it down in April, and the threshold reverted. That episode is worth remembering for two reasons: the wealth tax is the lever Colombian governments reach for first, and the court is the backstop that decides how far they get.

What to do about it, which is mostly nothing

Do not restructure anything on the strength of an inaugural speech. Between an announcement and a promulgated law sit a filed bill, two chambers, committee stages and, in Colombia, a reasonable chance of a Constitutional Court challenge. The previous administration’s reform cleared none of that.

What is worth doing now is knowing your own position. Count your days honestly across the rolling year, not the calendar year. Know whether your net worth would sit above or below the current threshold. For 2026 that line is 72,000 UVT, and with the UVT fixed at COP 52,374 for the year it works out to about COP 3.77 billion, or roughly US$1.19 million at Friday’s rate. Above it the rate starts at 0.5 percent and rises in bands. The threshold is written in UVT rather than pesos precisely so that it moves with inflation every January, which means a portfolio that sits comfortably below the line one year can cross it the next without you doing anything at all. If you are close to either line, that is a conversation with a Colombian accountant, not a decision to take from a news story.

The other thing worth watching is the offset. A government that removes a tax and freezes spending in the same week has to find the money somewhere, and the same speech promised mega-prisons and a harder security posture, neither of which is cheap. What replaces the wealth tax in the reform bill will tell you more than its removal does.

The wider signal

Read this alongside what the outgoing government did in its final fortnight. On 4 August the environment ministry signed a resolution closing 42 percent of the country to new mining and oil contracts. On 20 July it filed a bill to ban fracking outright. Within three weeks Colombia has produced both of those and a new president promising the opposite on both counts.

For anyone modelling Colombian exposure, the lesson is not which side wins. It is that Colombian tax and resource policy now changes with the political cycle rather than through settled law, and that instruments made by decree or resolution can be unmade the same way. Price the volatility, not the position. This is general information, not tax or legal advice.

The Short Version In short: Your LatAm expat and nomad daily guide for Saturday, August 8. Colombia’s new president used his first hours to promise the abolition of the wealth tax and to re-authorise fracking, and a weak US jobs report pushed the Mexican peso to a five-month high and the Peruvian sol to a four-month high. 01 Colombia’s opening move. Abelardo De La Espriella says the wealth tax will go, announced a spending-freeze decree and confirmed fracking will be re-authorised. All of it is announced, none of it is law. 02 The dollar slipped. US payrolls fell 23,000 in July against a consensus of about +80,000, and September rate-hike odds dropped from roughly 57 to 44 percent. 03 This weekend. Medellín’s Desfile de Silleteros closes the Feria on Sunday afternoon, and Cali opens the 30th Petronio Álvarez the same day. What changed since yesterdayColombia moved from ceremony to policy: the new government named the wealth tax as its first target and confirmed fracking will return. The US jobs report came in far weaker than expected, lifting the peso and the sol. Argentina went the other way, with country risk climbing to 451 while the rest of the region rallied.

Good morning. Your LatAm expat nomad daily guide opens on what Colombia’s new government said it will do to taxes, a soft US jobs number that moved every currency in the region, and a weekend of parades.

01 Visas & Residency

Where What changed What it means for you Colombia The new government says it will abolish the wealth tax as the centrepiece of a structural tax reform, and announced a decree freezing public spending. Nothing has passed Congress. The wealth tax is the levy that catches foreign tax residents on worldwide assets above the threshold, so this is the single biggest change to the calculus of becoming a Colombian tax resident in years — if it survives Congress. Do not restructure anything on an announcement. Colombia Fracking will be re-authorised under what the president called responsible and sustainable technical standards. Nothing for your visa. It matters for energy costs and for anyone with upstream exposure, and it will draw an immediate court challenge. Region-wide No visa or residency rule changed anywhere in the region on Friday or overnight. The rules that bind you today are the ones that bound you last week — Argentina’s border insurance check, Brazil and Panama’s insurance conditions on visas, and the tighter tourist-stay enforcement across the region.

02 Cost of Living & Money

Markets are closed for the weekend, so the rates below are Friday’s close — except the Colombian peso, where the official rate is set daily and carries through today. The direction of travel came from Washington: US payrolls fell 23,000 in July against a consensus of about 80,000 gains, with May and June revised down by a combined 103,000 and participation at a five-year low of 61.4 percent. The dollar sagged and every currency in the region firmed.

Currency Per US$ Read Brazilian real 5.09 firmer on the US data Mexican peso 17.14 five-month high for the peso; intraday 17.09 Colombian peso 3,157 official rate in force today Chilean peso 915 barely moved Peruvian sol 3.38 four-month low for the dollar Argentine peso 1,520 retail; blue near 1,525, CCL near 1,579 Uruguayan peso 40.25 stable

If you earn in dollars and spend in pesos or soles, this is the worst level since March in Mexico and since April in Peru. If you have a local obligation you were planning to fund, the arithmetic just got worse. The Fed is on hold at 3.50 to 3.75 percent, and the market cut the odds of a September hike from about 57 percent to about 44 after the jobs print — an unusual direction for this region to be reading. Mexico’s Banxico held at 6.50 percent on Thursday, its second hold in a row.

Argentina is the exception and it is worth watching. Country risk closed at 451 basis points, up 3 percent on the day and the highest since June, with the Merval down for a sixth straight session while Wall Street rallied. The blue-dollar gap has collapsed to under half a percent, but the CCL gap has widened to about 5.6 percent — the tell that the pressure is on institutional money leaving rather than retail.

03 What’s On

Sunday is the big day. Medellín’s Feria de las Flores closes with the Desfile de Silleteros, 2 p.m. to 7 p.m., in its 69th edition, with around 700 silleteros carrying flower arrangements that can weigh over 100 kilos along a 2.4-kilometre route. Get there early and check the route on the day — local outlets are giving different versions of it.

Cali opens the 30th Festival Petronio Álvarez the same day with the commemorative parade “Bundeando pa’ la Casa Grande”, with more than 1,600 participants from 23 Pacific-coast colonias. The main programme — the music competition, the traditional-expressions showcase and the Caserío Pacífico — runs 12 to 17 August at the Unidad Deportiva Alberto Galindo.

In Brazil, Sunday is Dia dos Pais. Restaurants in Rio and São Paulo will be full and reservations scarce, so book today if you have not. São Paulo also has the Heritage Festival and the Festa de Nossa Senhora Achiropita, the Italian street festival in Bixiga. In Mexico City, the Festival de Culturas Indígenas, Pueblos y Barrios Originarios is running free in the Zócalo until 23 August, with a large food pavilion.

04 Art & Culture

The Petronio is the cultural event of the Colombian year for anyone interested in Afro-Pacific music, and the 30th edition adds a Global Afro-Diasporic Summit and an anniversary exhibition. If you are in Cali this week, the free programming around the Unidad Deportiva is the part most visitors miss.

Medellín’s silleteros are the older tradition — campesino flower growers from Santa Elena who once carried their stock into the city on their backs, now carrying arrangements as artworks. It is the one day of the year the city genuinely stops.

05 Food & Coffee

Two practical notes. In São Paulo and Rio, Father’s Day Sunday is the single busiest restaurant day of the Brazilian winter — if you want a table anywhere good, today is the last realistic moment to book. And in Cali, the Caserío Pacífico at the Petronio is the best week of the year to eat Pacific-coast food outside the coast itself, from encocados to viche.

06 Community & Safety

Brazil. The cyclone has moved out to sea, but INMET’s windstorm alert runs through today across eleven states including Rio, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo, with gusts of up to 100 km/h possible on the Rio and São Paulo coasts. The Port of Santos channel was shut for about 90 minutes on Friday and ferry services were halted. Expect residual delays at Santos Dumont and Congonhas and rough seas. The serious damage was in Rio Grande do Sul on Thursday: one person killed, five injured, 118 municipalities reporting damage, more than 1,800 people out of their homes and around 229,000 properties still without power on Friday afternoon.

Cali. The drone ban over Cali and neighbouring municipalities runs until 11:59 p.m. tonight, enforced with anti-drone systems, and downtown road closures hold through today. If you are heading to Sunday’s Petronio parade, expect closures to be lifting only through Sunday morning. Our guide to the Cali restrictions has the detail.

07 What to Watch — August 8–17

Sat Aug 8 Drone ban over Cali and neighbours ends at 11:59 p.m.; INMET wind alert across eleven Brazilian states.

Sun Aug 9 Medellín’s Desfile de Silleteros, 2 p.m.; Cali opens the 30th Petronio Álvarez; Dia dos Pais in Brazil.

Tue Aug 11 Brazil’s IPCA inflation for July, from IBGE at noon. Inflation is running 3.36 percent year to date against 4.26 percent for all of 2025.

Wed Aug 12 Brazil retail trade survey; the Petronio main programme opens at the Unidad Deportiva Alberto Galindo in Cali.

Thu Aug 13 Argentina’s INDEC inflation for July, 4 p.m. Consensus is around 2.0 percent on the month. This one feeds straight into rent indexation, pensions and UVA loan balances. Colombia’s cabinet meets in La Guajira.

Mon Aug 17 Festival Petronio Álvarez closes in Cali.

Global Economy Briefing Saturday, August 8, 2026

The US economy shed 23,000 jobs in July, yet the S&P 500 closed at a record as investors read the weak report as ruling out a Federal Reserve rate rise.

Rio Times Global Economy Briefing

The Big Three America lost jobs. The economy unexpectedly shed 23,000 jobs in July, against forecasts of an 80,000 gain — a startling reversal that reshaped expectations for interest rates.

The economy unexpectedly shed jobs in July, against forecasts of an 80,000 gain — a startling reversal that reshaped expectations for interest rates. Records anyway. The S&P 500 closed at an all-time high and the Nasdaq jumped 1.3%, as a weak labour market convinced investors the Fed will hold rates rather than raise them.

The S&P 500 closed at an all-time high and the Nasdaq jumped 1.3%, as a weak labour market convinced investors the Fed will hold rates rather than raise them. A gift for Brazil. A softer US outlook pulled the dollar and bond yields down, while at home wholesale prices fell further and foreign bets on the real climbed sharply.

01 America loses jobs, and Wall Street cheers

The most important number of the month landed with a jolt. The United States economy actually shed 23,000 jobs in July, a stark miss against forecasts of an 80,000 gain and the first monthly decline in years. Wages cooled too, rising just 3.2% over the year, below expectations.

Ordinarily a shrinking jobs market would frighten investors. Instead, stocks rallied to fresh records — the S&P 500 closed at an all-time high, the Nasdaq jumped 1.3%, and even smaller companies advanced. The logic was simple: a weak labour market takes the pressure off the Federal Reserve, and investors quickly concluded that a rate rise, feared only weeks ago, is now firmly off the table.

Bond yields and the dollar fell as traders repriced the outlook for cheaper money, while gold jumped 2.11% and the market’s fear gauge sank to unusually calm levels. It was a near-perfect mirror image of early June, when a blockbuster jobs report sent shares tumbling on fears of higher rates. The same machinery, running in reverse, this time delivered a celebration.

02 A weaker dollar hands Brazil an opening

For Brazil, few developments are as welcome as a Federal Reserve expected to hold or lower rates. When American rates look set to fall, the dollar softens and higher-yielding markets like Brazil become more attractive — and the market’s response on Friday, with the dollar and US yields sliding, pointed exactly that way.

The domestic backdrop is strengthening the case. Brazilian wholesale prices fell again in July, a monthly drop of 0.86% that deepened an existing deflation, while car production rebounded. Across the region the story rhymed: Mexican core inflation slipped below 4% for the first time in months. With inflation fading at home and the external threat from US rates easing, Brazil’s central bank has room to keep lowering the Selic rate from its current 14.00%.

Investors are already positioning for it. Foreign bets on the real climbing in value jumped sharply last week, reaching their highest in months — a clear signal that global money expects the currency to strengthen as the interest-rate gap with the United States narrows in Brazil’s favour. After a year in which the hawkish Fed was the chief obstacle, a cooling US jobs market may prove the moment the balance tips toward Brazil.

03 The paradox — unemployment fell because workers vanished

Buried in the jobs report was a genuine riddle. Even as the economy lost jobs, the unemployment rate did not rise — it fell, to 4.1%. On its face that looks like good news layered on bad, but the explanation is far less comforting.

The rate fell because people stopped looking for work altogether, and those no longer searching are not counted as unemployed. The share of Americans in the workforce slipped to 61.4%, and nearly 1.4 million people have left the labour force this year alone. A jobless rate that improves because the workforce is shrinking is a statistical mirage, not a sign of health. It also hands the Federal Reserve a genuine dilemma: the falling unemployment rate hints at a stable jobs market, while the outright loss of jobs points to a weakening one. Which signal the central bank chooses to believe will shape its next move — and the market has already placed its bet on the gloomier reading.

04 What to watch today and this week

Next week: US consumer price figures, the next major test of whether inflation is cool enough to let the Federal Reserve ease.

US consumer price figures, the next major test of whether inflation is cool enough to let the Federal Reserve ease. This week: Comments from Fed officials, for signs of how seriously they take the surprise drop in employment.

Comments from Fed officials, for signs of how seriously they take the surprise drop in employment. This week: The path of the dollar and US bond yields, the clearest gauges of shifting rate expectations and the main channel to Brazil.

The path of the dollar and US bond yields, the clearest gauges of shifting rate expectations and the main channel to Brazil. Ahead: Whether foreign inflows into Brazil and other emerging markets accelerate as bets on US rate cuts grow.

Whether foreign inflows into Brazil and other emerging markets accelerate as bets on US rate cuts grow. Ahead: Oil prices, hovering near $77, as fresh talks on Iran influence the outlook for global inflation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did stocks rise when the jobs report was so weak?

Because a weak labour market makes the Federal Reserve less likely to raise interest rates, and possibly more likely to cut them. Lower rates reduce borrowing costs and make shares more attractive, especially fast-growing technology companies. Investors judged that the loss of 23,000 jobs all but removes the threat of a rate rise that had worried markets, so they bought shares — sending the S&P 500 to a record. It is a case of apparently bad economic news being treated as good news for markets.

How can unemployment fall while the economy loses jobs?

The two figures come from different surveys and measure different things. The unemployment rate only counts people who are actively looking for work. In July, the rate fell to 4.1% not because more people found jobs, but because many stopped searching and left the workforce entirely — the participation rate dropped to 61.4%. People who are not looking are not counted as unemployed, so the rate can fall even as the number of jobs declines. It is a sign of a discouraged workforce, not a strong one.

What does a softer US jobs market mean for Brazil?

It is broadly positive. When the US economy weakens and the Federal Reserve is expected to lower rates, the dollar tends to soften and investors look for higher returns in emerging markets like Brazil. This supports the real and can attract foreign capital. Combined with falling inflation at home — Brazilian wholesale prices dropped again in July — it gives Brazil’s central bank more room to keep cutting its own interest rate, while a narrower rate gap with the US still leaves Brazil offering attractive returns.

Why are foreign bets on the real rising?

Investors use certain financial contracts to bet on whether a currency will strengthen or weaken. Last week those positions shifted sharply toward the real strengthening, reaching their highest in months. The reasoning is that as the US Federal Reserve moves toward cutting rates while Brazil’s inflation falls under control, the gap between the two countries’ rates works in Brazil’s favour, making the real more appealing. Rising bets of this kind often precede, and can help drive, actual gains in the currency.

Does this weak report guarantee a US rate cut?

Not necessarily. While markets have taken a near-term rate rise off the table, the picture is mixed. The economy lost jobs, which argues for easier policy, but the unemployment rate fell, which some Fed officials may read as a sign the labour market is still stable. The central bank will weigh both signals along with upcoming inflation data before deciding. So while the report makes a rate rise far less likely, it does not by itself lock in a cut — the coming weeks of data will be decisive.

a pause after Thursday’s close at the highest level since April The week still finished 2.18% higher, making Chile the region’s strongest performer over the five sessions

as Cencosud dropped 0.49% after posting a quarterly loss and CMPC saw profits fall 89% from a year earlier The dollar sank at the open, losing close to 10 pesos — though it closed down just 3.81, at 912.03 — after the United States reported a contraction of 23,000 jobs in July

Today’s Focus Chile spent the week doing everything right and then stopped to catch its breath. Inflation came in lower, the government’s reconstruction package passed, and the IPSA closed Thursday at its highest since April. Friday brought a marginal fall of 0.17%. The reason was partly caution ahead of the weekend and partly two large companies reporting figures the market did not like. None of that spoiled the week. The index still finished 2.18% higher, the best showing in Latin America over the five sessions. What matters today. Chile is the one market in the region whose gains this week came from its own economy rather than from an American data release.
