01 The session in one read

The IPSA eased 0.17% on Friday, a marginal decline that followed a week of solid gains. Over the five sessions the index rose 2.18%, and it came into Friday having closed at its best level since April.

The morning suggested otherwise. The index opened 0.5% higher at 11,327.42 points, led by Santander at 2.1%, Bci at 1.5% and the lithium producer SQM-B at 1.5%, all heavyweight names.

It gave that back through the day. Diario Financiero described a market waiting for weekend news on the Middle East, while volatility widened in the United States after the July employment figures.

Two company reports did the rest. Cencosud fell 0.49% after a quarterly loss, and CMPC finished flat after profits collapsed, which took the shine off an otherwise constructive week.

Assessment — A pause, not a turn MEDIUM The distinction that matters is where Chile’s week came from. Mexico rose on an American data release and Brazil fell on the same one, but Chile advanced on domestic news: inflation falling from 4.3% to 3.5%, an earnings season delivering operational surprises, and a reconstruction package with tax reductions that the market read favourably. A 0.17% decline on the final day, driven by two identifiable company results and by caution before a weekend of geopolitical headlines, does not undo that. The variable to watch is copper, which eased on Friday and remains the single largest external influence on Chilean assets.

02 The week’s numbers

Measure Level Change Read S&P IPSA, Friday — −0.17% Marginal fall after Thursday’s April high S&P IPSA, week — +2.18% Best performer in Latin America Thursday’s close 11,275.15 +1.05% Highest level since April USD/CLP 912.03 −0.42% Fell close to 10 pesos at the open, pared to 3.8 by the close Annual inflation, July 3.5% from 4.3% Monthly rise of 0.1%, below the 0.2% expected Copper — −2.1% Eased on Friday; Chile’s largest export

The inflation figure is the number of the week. A fall from 4.3% to 3.5% in a single month is a large move, and by The Rio Times’ calculation it takes the annual rate 0.8 percentage points closer to the central bank’s 3% target.

The equity move should be read alongside it. An index that gains 2.18% in a week when inflation drops and a stimulus package passes is behaving rationally rather than speculatively.

03 Why it moved — good domestic news, then a pause for the weekend

The week’s foundation was laid at home. July consumer prices rose 0.1% from June, below the 0.2% expected, and the twelve-month inflation rate slowed from 4.3% to 3.5%.

Politics helped rather than hindered, which is not always the case. Parliament approved the government’s National Reconstruction Project, whose tax reductions and other stimulus measures were generally well received by market participants.

Earnings season added a third leg. Diario Financiero noted that results had brought positive operational surprises, and that combination carried the index to its best close since April on Thursday.

Friday interrupted the sequence for two reasons. The first was external: traders were waiting to see what emerged from the Middle East over the weekend, with the Strait of Hormuz still the dominant geopolitical question.

The second was corporate. Cencosud reported a loss of 36,500 million pesos for the second quarter when the market had on average expected a profit of 67,200 million, and the shares fell 0.49%.

CMPC gave a variation on the same theme. It sold more than expected in the quarter to June, but earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of nearly US$270 million came in below consensus and profits fell 89% from a year earlier to US$8.7 million.

04 The day’s movers

Driver Level / Move Change Note Santander Chile (BSANTANDER) — −1.11% Led at the open, then gave it all back Bci (BCI) — +1.5% Second bank among the early leaders SQM-B (SQM-B) — −0.77% Lithium producer; opened higher, closed lower CMPC (CMPC) — 0.0% Profits down 89% to US$8.7m; sales beat Cencosud (CENCOSUD) — −0.49% Quarterly loss of CLP 36,500m against expected profit

The opening leaderboard and the closing one told different stories. Santander, Bci and SQM-B all rose more than 1.5% in early trading, and between them they carry enough weight to lift the whole index.

The retail side pulled the other way. Cencosud’s loss was the session’s clearest negative, and its chief executive warned of aggressive competition in the Chilean market, which matters more for the sector’s outlook than the single quarter does.

CMPC is the more interesting case. The forestry group beat on revenue but missed on operating profit, and the 89% fall in net earnings shows how much pressure pulp and paper prices have put on margins.

05 The peso and the copper link

The dollar fell sharply at the open, losing close to 10 pesos after the United States reported that employers had cut 23,000 jobs in July against expectations of an 80,000 gain. The dollar pared most of that, settling at 912.03 pesos, a fall of 3.81 pesos or 0.42% on the day.

The mechanism runs through two channels at once. A weaker dollar lifts most emerging currencies, and lower American rate expectations reduce the pull of dollar assets.

For Chile there is a third channel that matters more than either. Copper is the country’s largest export, and the metal’s price sets the terms for export earnings, mining profits and, ultimately, the currency.

That link cut against the peso on Friday. Copper eased about 2.1% on Friday, having been higher earlier in the week, which takes some of the support away.

The inflation data works in the currency’s favour on a longer view. With the annual rate down to 3.5%, the pressure on the central bank has eased considerably from where it stood at the start of the year.

06 The regional scoreboard

Index Country Change IPC Mexico +0.82% IPSA Chile −0.17% Merval Argentina −0.45% Ibovespa Brazil −1.73% COLCAP Colombia closed

Friday was a day of small moves everywhere except Brazil. Mexico rose 0.82% because its market reads American data as its own, while the Ibovespa fell 1.73% as investors moved money out of emerging markets and into American technology shares.

Chile’s 0.17% decline sits closer to Argentina’s 0.45% fall than to either extreme, but the weekly picture is what separates them. Chile gained 2.18% over the five sessions while Argentina fell for a sixth consecutive day, and Colombia did not trade at all on Friday because of the Battle of Boyacá holiday.

07 The technical picture

The index has spent the week reclaiming ground it lost earlier in the summer, and Thursday’s close was the highest since April. That makes the April peak the reference point that now matters rather than any nearby round number.

Friday’s decline was too small to signal anything on its own. A single 0.17% move after a 2.18% week is noise, and the pattern only becomes meaningful if the pause extends into the coming sessions without a clear external trigger.

The genuine risk sits outside the chart. Copper eased on Friday and the Middle East remains unresolved, so the index enters next week with its domestic story intact and its external one open.

08 What to watch

Copper: The metal eased on Friday and remains the single biggest external influence on Chilean shares and the peso.

World.title: Mexican Stocks Jump as Weak US Jobs Data Lifts Miners and Peso
World.content:
Editor’s note, 9 August 2026. An earlier version put the peso’s close at 17.12 per dollar and called it the strongest level since 18 February. Banxico-referenced reporting puts the close at 17.14 against 17.21 on Thursday. The February comparison does not hold: the 18 February close was 17.13, firmer than Friday’s. The level, the size of the move and the superlative have all been corrected.

Key Facts Mexico’s S&P/BMV IPC rose 0.82% to 66,938.64 points, a gain of 542.49 points that ended a run of four losses in five sessions

a gain of 542.49 points that ended a run of four losses in five sessions The peso closed at about 17.14 per dollar, firmer on the day, after a weak United States jobs report knocked the dollar lower

firmer on the day, after a weak United States jobs report knocked the dollar lower Mining names led the advance, with Peñoles and Grupo México riding a precious-metals rally that took gold 2.11% higher

with Peñoles and Grupo México riding a precious-metals rally that took gold 2.11% higher Mexico’s central bank held its rate at 6.50% on Thursday, a unanimous second consecutive pause, and pushed its inflation target date out to late 2027

a unanimous second consecutive pause, and pushed its inflation target date out to late 2027 The single session wiped out August’s losses, leaving the index roughly flat for the month after being down 0.81% a day earlier

Today’s Focus Mexican shares had their best day in weeks on Friday, and the reason came from Washington. American employers shed jobs in July instead of adding them, and a market that trades in step with the United States took that as good news.

The S&P/BMV IPC climbed 0.82% to 66,938.64 points, adding 542.49 points and breaking a run of four falls in five sessions. The peso went with it, firming against a broadly weaker dollar.

The gains were concentrated where the dollar’s weakness bites hardest. Precious metals rallied, and Mexico’s big miners carried the index.

What matters today. The same American jobs number that pushed money out of Brazil pushed it into Mexico, which is the clearest illustration this year of how differently the region’s two largest markets are wired.

Mexico’s IPC and the day on the BMV. (Photo internet reproduction)

01 The session in one read

The IPC finished Friday at 66,938.64 points, up 542.49 or 0.82%, on volume of 113,357,974. It was the index’s first convincing session in a week that had otherwise been a slow drift lower.

The shape of the day was one-directional. The index opened at 66,394.89, which was also its low, ran to 67,185.88 at the top and gave back only part of that into the close.

The turn was imported. United States employers cut 23,000 jobs in July against forecasts of an 80,000 gain, and June was revised down to just 20,000, which pushed expectations of a Federal Reserve rate rise from September into October.

Wall Street rose on that reading and Mexico followed, with the Dow up 0.28%, the S&P 500 up 0.62% and the Nasdaq up 1.30%. Brazil, wired differently, fell 1.73% on the same news.

Assessment — The right side of a weak American number MEDIUM Mexico benefits twice from a soft United States labour report: the dollar falls, which lifts the peso and the metals its miners dig, and the rate outlook softens, which lifts everything else. That is why Friday’s gain was led by Peñoles and Grupo México rather than by anything domestic. The caution is that none of this originated in Mexico, so the durability of the move depends on American data rather than on the local economy, and the index is still 0.8% below where it sat in late July.

02 The day’s numbers

Measure Level Change Read S&P/BMV IPC 66,938.64 +0.82% +542.49 points; best session in weeks Session range 66,394.89 — 67,185.88 — Opened at the low and held the gain USD/MXN 17.14 −0.41% Peso firmer against a weaker dollar Central bank rate 6.50% — Held Thursday; second consecutive pause Mexican 10-year yield 9.15% — Against 4.65% on the US 10-year July inflation 3.12% −0.25 pp Down from 3.37%, in line with forecasts

The month had been going badly until Friday. Mexican shares were down 0.81% for August as of Thursday, according to Actinver, and the 0.82% gain almost exactly cancels that—leaving August essentially flat, by The Rio Times’ calculation.

For the year the index remains modestly ahead. It was up 3.25% for 2026 through Thursday, a return that Friday’s session improves but does not transform.

03 Why it moved — a weak American jobs report cut in Mexico’s favour

Mexico’s market is tied more tightly to the United States than any other in Latin America, and on Friday that paid. The employment report was genuinely poor, and poor American data currently means a lower chance of higher American interest rates.

The dollar fell across the board on that reading. A broad index measuring the dollar against six developed-market currencies dropped 0.33%, and emerging-market currencies rallied with the South African rand, the South Korean won and the Russian rouble all gaining more than 0.9%.

For Mexico the effect compounds. A weaker dollar lifts precious metals, and precious metals are a large part of what the Mexican index actually contains.

Local conditions helped rather than hindered. Mexico’s central bank had held its rate at 6.50% the day before in a unanimous decision, its second straight pause since June, and July inflation came in at 3.12% against 3.37% previously.

That combination—steady local rates, easing local inflation, falling American rate expectations—is close to ideal for Mexican assets. The gap between the Mexican ten-year yield at 9.15% and the American equivalent at 4.65% does the rest of the work in pulling money in.

The one discordant note came from oil, which fell on Friday as talk resurfaced of a deal between Gulf states and Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. That matters less for Mexico than for its oil-exporting neighbours.

04 The day’s movers

Driver Level / Move Change Note Industrias Peñoles (PE&OLES) — +3.68% Session’s sharpest move; silver and gold miner Grupo México (GMEXICO) — +2.58% Copper and metals; rode the same rally Becle (CUERVO) — +1.66% Consumer name lifted by broader risk appetite GCC (GCC) — +1.64% Cement maker with heavy US exposure Cemex (CEMEX) — +0.31% Steadied after a 2.11% fall on Thursday América Móvil (AMX) — −0.92% Heavyweight that sat out the advance

The leaderboard was a metals story from top to bottom. Peñoles, which mines silver and gold, was the sharpest riser in the index, and Grupo México followed it up—both tracking a precious-metals rally that carried gold 2.11% higher on the day.

Away from mining the gains were broader but thinner. Becle, the tequila producer, and the cement maker GCC each added close to 2%, while the Bolsa Mexicana de Valores itself rose 1.54%.

The decliners were few. América Móvil eased 0.92%, leaving the index’s heaviest name out of step with the rest of the market, while Cemex edged up 0.31% after a 2.11% fall on Thursday.

Thursday had been the mirror image. The index lost 0.19% to close at its lowest since 24 July, dragged by Volaris down 3.99%, Cemex down 2.11%, Femsa down 2.17% and Gruma down 1.37%.

05 The peso and the rate gap

The peso closed at roughly 17.14 per dollar against Thursday’s 17.21, a gain of about four-tenths of a per cent.

The mechanism is not complicated. Mexico’s central bank is holding at 6.50% while the United States has been cutting, and money moves toward the higher return as long as the currency looks stable.

Thursday’s decision reinforced that. The board voted unanimously to hold for a second consecutive meeting, and it delayed to the final quarter of 2027 the point at which it expects inflation to settle back at the 3% target—which markets read as a promise to keep rates high for longer.

The peso has been on this path for a while. The dollar has now fallen for four consecutive sessions against it and is down more than 8% over the past twelve months, having traded above 17.60 as recently as late July.

Analysts are not calling it a verdict on the economy. As one Mexican outlet put it this week, the peso’s advance reflects the yield gap and global dollar weakness rather than any improvement in domestic growth.

Forecasts for the end of 2026 still sit above Friday’s level, which means the consensus expects at least some of this strength to unwind before the year is out.

06 The regional scoreboard

Index Country Change IPC Mexico +0.82% IPSA Chile −0.17% Merval Argentina −0.45% Ibovespa Brazil −1.73% COLCAP Colombia closed

Mexico was the region’s only clear winner on Friday, and the contrast with Brazil is the point. The Ibovespa fell 1.73% as global investors rotated out of emerging markets and into American technology shares, while Mexico benefited from being read as an extension of the American cycle rather than an alternative to it.

Elsewhere the moves were small. Chile’s IPSA eased 0.17% after a week that still finished 2.18% higher, Argentina’s Merval fell 0.45% in a sixth consecutive decline, and Colombia did not trade at all—Friday was the Battle of Boyacá holiday, which is also when the country swore in its new president.

07 The technical picture

Friday’s close of 66,938.64 puts the index back above the 66,400 area that had capped it for most of the week, but it stops short of 67,000. That round number has turned the market away more than once since June.

The longer view is less encouraging. The index has been drifting sideways to lower since its highs in February, and the rising line that supported it through 2025 now sits just underneath the current level rather than comfortably below it. One strong session does not undo that pattern, particularly when the impetus came from a foreign data release.

08 What to watch

The next American data: Friday’s move was imported, so the follow-through depends on what United States figures say next about the rate path.

Friday’s move was imported, so the follow-through depends on what United States figures say next about the rate path. Precious metals: Peñoles and Grupo México did most of the lifting, and both live or die by the gold and silver price.

Peñoles and Grupo México did most of the lifting, and both live or die by the gold and silver price. The 67,000 mark: The index closed just below it; clearing it on volume would be the first real technical signal in weeks.

The index closed just below it; clearing it on volume would be the first real technical signal in weeks. The peso at 17.10: Analysts flagged 17.20 as the level to break, and it broke; the next tests sit at 17.10 and 17.05.

Analysts flagged 17.20 as the level to break, and it broke; the next tests sit at 17.10 and 17.05. Core inflation: Headline inflation eased to 3.12%, but the central bank’s caution rests on the underlying measure, which has been stickier.

World.content:

Editor’s note, 9 August 2026. An earlier version gave Bioceres a fall of 4.4 per cent in the movers table while the same article said the worst-hit Argentine shares in New York fell as much as 5.6 per cent, led by Bioceres. Bioceres fell 5.56 per cent. The table and the text have been reconciled.

Key Facts Argentina’s S&P Merval fell 0.45% to 3,086,784.5 points, a sixth consecutive decline that takes the index back to where it traded on 5 June

a sixth consecutive decline that takes the index back to where it traded on 5 June Country risk closed at 451 points, a rise of 3% in twenty-four hours and the highest reading since June

a rise of 3% in twenty-four hours and the highest reading since June Argentine shares in New York fell by as much as 5.6%, led by Bioceres, Corporación América and Loma Negra

led by Bioceres, Corporación América and Loma Negra The market decoupled from a strong global session, with Wall Street near record levels after a weak United States jobs report that Argentina did not share in

with Wall Street near record levels after a weak United States jobs report that Argentina did not share in Domestic data did the damage, with industrial output down 2.2% in the first half and construction down 4.1% in June, its fourth monthly fall

Today’s Focus Friday was a good day for almost every market except Argentina’s. A weak United States jobs report sent Wall Street back toward record levels and, in theory, handed emerging markets exactly the conditions they like. Buenos Aires did not join in. The S&P Merval fell 0.45% to 3,086,784.5 points, a sixth straight decline, while the premium investors demand to hold Argentine debt rose to its highest since June. The reason was local. Industrial output, construction and inflation figures all pointed the wrong way in the same week, and they outweighed the relief coming from abroad. What matters today. When a market cannot rally on the best global backdrop it has had in weeks, the problem is at home rather than in the world.

The Banco Central de la República Argentina in Buenos Aires. (Photo internet reproduction)

01 The session in one read

The Merval closed Friday at 3,086,784.5 points, down 0.45% from the previous session’s 3,100,731.8. It was the sixth consecutive fall in peso terms and left the index back at the level it last held on 5 June.

The day had a wide swing inside it. The index reached 3,149,198.9 at the top and 3,055,274.6 at the bottom before settling nearer the lower end, which is a spread of about 3% between the extremes.

Measured in dollars the picture is worse. The index has moved away from the 2,000-point barrier that had acted as a floor since 22 May, and August is now running at a loss approaching 6%.

The contrast with the rest of the world was the day’s defining feature. New York finished close to record highs after the American employment report, while Argentine bonds, shares and the risk premium all moved the other way.

Assessment — A decoupling that says more than the number MEDIUM The mechanics of Friday should have favoured Argentina: a weaker dollar and lower American rate expectations ease global financial conditions, make dollar assets less attractive and push investors toward higher-yielding markets, while cheaper external funding tends to compress sovereign spreads. None of that reached Buenos Aires, and country risk rose instead of falling. That gap between what the global backdrop offered and what Argentine assets delivered is the signal worth watching, because it suggests investors are pricing domestic activity and the money market rather than the international cycle.

02 The day’s numbers

03 Why it moved — a good global day that Argentina did not join

The starting point was American. Employers in the United States shed jobs in July rather than adding them, which cooled the labour market more than expected and shifted the outlook for Federal Reserve policy.

That reading usually helps countries like Argentina. A softer dollar and lower American rates loosen global financial conditions, reduce the appeal of holding dollars and push money toward riskier markets, while cheaper external funding tends to narrow the spread on government debt.

It did not happen. Argentine sovereign bonds in dollars fell, the shares traded in New York fell, and the risk premium widened rather than compressing.

The explanation came from three domestic figures released around the same time. The statistics agency reported that industrial production contracted 2.2% in the first half of 2026, and that construction fell 4.1% in June, its fourth consecutive monthly decline.

Inflation in the city of Buenos Aires then accelerated to 2.9% in July. Combined with tight conditions in the local money market, that pushed peso-denominated sovereign bonds broadly lower.

The central bank added a further note of firmness. It ruled out lowering the reserves banks must hold, said it would not intervene over rising loan arrears, and indicated it is counting on a recovery in credit to resolve the problem instead.

04 The day’s movers

The selling in New York was broader than the Buenos Aires index suggests, with the worst-hit Argentine shares down as much as 5.6%. Bioceres, an agricultural biotechnology company, led the decline at 5.6%.

Two of the three worst performers have a direct line to the domestic data. Corporación América runs airports and Loma Negra makes cement, so both sit squarely in the activity numbers that disappointed this week.

The bond market moved in the same direction for a different reason. Analysts pointed to the money market rather than to any single company, with tight peso liquidity and the Buenos Aires inflation print pushing local-currency debt lower across the board.

05 The peso and the risk premium

The currency was the quiet part of the day. The wholesale rate closed around 1,498.50 pesos per dollar, down about 1.25 pesos, and the official rate at Banco Nación did not move at all from 1,470 to buy and 1,520 to sell.

The parallel rates drifted the other way. The financial dollar used to move money offshore rose about 0.6% to roughly 1,581 pesos, while the stock-market dollar gained around 0.4% to about 1,526.

The risk premium is where the pressure showed. At 451 points it is 3% higher than a day earlier and back to levels last seen in June, having spent recent weeks approaching the psychologically important 400 mark from above.

Forecasts still point to a gradual, controlled slide rather than a break. The central bank’s monthly survey of analysts put the average wholesale rate for August at 1,512 pesos and the December figure at 1,652.

That December projection was cut by 20.70 pesos from the previous month’s survey. If it holds, the wholesale dollar would end the year 14.1% above December 2025—far below expected inflation over the same period, which means a further real appreciation of the peso.

The central bank has also been shoring up its position. It renewed its currency swap with China this week and extended the term from three years to five, which it framed as a move for greater predictability.

06 The regional scoreboard

Index Country Change IPC Mexico +0.82% IPSA Chile −0.17% Merval Argentina −0.45% Ibovespa Brazil −1.73% COLCAP Colombia closed

The region split on how closely each market tracks the United States. Mexico rose 0.82% because a softer American rate outlook reads straight through to a market tied to the American cycle, and it was the only clear gainer.

Argentina and Brazil both fell, but for different reasons. Brazil lost 1.73% as global investors moved money out of emerging markets and into American technology shares, while Argentina’s decline was domestic. Chile eased 0.17% after a week that still finished 2.18% higher, and Colombia did not trade at all, with Friday being the Battle of Boyacá holiday.

07 The technical picture

The Merval has now fallen six sessions in a row and sits at 3,086,784.5, back where it traded on 5 June. That erases two months of progress and puts the index roughly 9% below its July record.

The dollar-denominated reading is the one long-term investors watch, and it has slipped away from 2,000 points, a level that held as a floor from 22 May onward. Losing that support is more meaningful than the peso number, because it strips out the effect of inflation on the index.

The rising line that has guided the index since late last year still runs beneath the current level, so the longer trend is not yet broken. But six consecutive down sessions on a day when the global backdrop was helpful is the kind of pattern that tends to need a domestic catalyst to reverse.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the S&P Merval?

It is Argentina’s main stock index, tracking the most heavily traded companies on the Buenos Aires exchange. Because Argentine inflation is high, the index is quoted in millions of pesos.

Why did Argentine shares fall when Wall Street rose?

A weak United States jobs report lifted American shares and would normally help emerging markets too. Argentine assets went the other way because domestic figures dominated: weak industrial and construction data, faster inflation in Buenos Aires city and tight conditions in the local money market.

What is country risk and why does it matter?

It measures the extra return investors demand to hold Argentine government debt rather than United States debt. It closed Friday at 451 points, up 3% in a day and the highest since June, which signals renewed caution about Argentina rather than about the world.

What happened to the peso?

Very little. The wholesale rate, which is the market’s reference, ended around 1,498.50 per dollar, a fall of about 1.25 pesos, while the official bank rate was unchanged at 1,520 for sale.

What are ADRs?

They are shares in Argentine companies traded in dollars in New York. They fell by as much as 5.6% on Friday, led by Bioceres, Corporacion America and Loma Negra.

World.title: Costa Rica Studies Monorail or Tram for Main Airport
World.content:
Costa Rican transportation officials are looking for European funding to study a public transit connection between Juan Santamaría International Airport and the planned electric train network. The proposal would connect the airport terminal with the railway line near Río Segundo, removing one of the main barriers facing travelers who want to use public transportation between the San Jose airport and the Greater Metropolitan Area.

Officials are considering several possible systems, including a monorail or light rail service. The technical studies would determine which option is best suited to the short connection, as well as its cost, design and possible construction timeline. The Costa Rican Railway Institute (Incofer), is developing the plan with the Ministry of Public Works and Transportation and Aeris, the company that manages Juan Santamaría International Airport.

The agencies hope to finance the studies through non-repayable cooperation funds from the European Union. However, the funding has not yet been confirmed, and authorities have not established how much the studies or eventual construction would cost. Transportation officials expect to get approval to begin the studies in December 2026.

The airport connection would link to the planned TIBI electric train project. From Río Segundo, passengers could continue by rail toward Alajuela, Heredia, San José and Cartago. Officials also want the transit system coordinated with the planned expansion of the highway between San José and San Ramón. That road project includes a new interchange in front of the airport designed to bring together cars, buses, trains and other forms of transportation.

A survey conducted among Costa Rican and international travelers found that 82 percent of respondents would be willing to use a public transportation connection at the airport if one were available. Juan Santamaría currently has public buses serving San José, Alajuela and other destinations, but the terminal does not have a direct rail connection. Many arriving passengers instead depend on taxis, ride-hailing services, rental cars or private hotel transfers.

The gap is particularly noticeable for visitors traveling into San José, where congestion along the General Cañas Highway can make travel times unpredictable. A rail connection has been discussed previously, but the latest proposal remains at an early stage. No technology has been selected, no construction funding has been approved and no opening date has been announced.

The studies will determine whether the project is technically and financially practical before the government decides whether to move ahead.

World.title: FIFA Defends Gianni Infantino Amid Leadership Crisis
World.content:
FIFA has accused critics of waging a “concerted and ongoing effort” to undermine the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino, as the crisis surrounding his leadership continues to deepen. The governing body issued a strongly worded statement Saturday defending Infantino following the collapse of a controversial proposal to bring private investors into FIFA’s World Cup commercial business.

The plan triggered fierce opposition from several major football organizations and has left Infantino facing boycott threats, calls for his resignation and growing questions about his bid for another term as FIFA president. Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, is seeking reelection at the organization’s congress in March 2027. FIFA’s 211 member associations will ultimately decide whether he remains in office.

European football’s governing body UEFA has emerged as one of his strongest critics. Despite FIFA abandoning the private investment proposal, UEFA has said the decision alone is not enough to restore confidence in Infantino’s leadership. The dispute has escalated to the point that European football officials have threatened to boycott FIFA competitions, including World Cups.

New Allegations Add to Pressure

Infantino faced another controversy Friday after The Telegraph reported allegations involving his time as UEFA general secretary between 2009 and 2016. The British newspaper alleged that Infantino used his influence to help secure the promotion of a female UEFA employee with whom he was reportedly involved in a personal relationship.

Infantino has categorically denied the allegations. The Telegraph also reported that the employee later received a six-figure payment when she left UEFA, along with approximately €50,000 ($57,800) toward an MBA program. UEFA has acknowledged that a payment was made to the former employee and that expenses connected with an MBA program were also covered.

FIFA did not specifically identify the Telegraph report in its Saturday statement but pushed back strongly against recent coverage surrounding its president. “Recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its president,” the organization said. FIFA added that speculation and insinuation should not be treated as fact and said it would challenge inaccurate or misleading reporting.

FIFA Warns Against Attempts to Remove Infantino

FIFA also emphasized that any effort to replace Infantino must follow the organization’s statutes and established election procedures. “Those who do not have the support of FIFA’s Member Associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA’s established democratic processes,” the organization said.

FIFA’s leadership reaffirmed its support for Infantino during a crisis meeting in Morocco earlier this week. The organization also apologized to its 211 member associations for mistakes in the way the private investment proposal was handled, acknowledging that members should have been more involved in the process.

That apology has done little to settle the dispute. UEFA has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation president Lise Klaveness went further Friday and publicly called for him to resign. Klaveness, one of Infantino’s most outspoken critics in international football, said he no longer has the institutional trust necessary to lead FIFA.

Her name has also been mentioned as a possible future candidate for the FIFA presidency, although she has played down speculation about running.

Infantino Retains Support Outside Europe

Despite the growing pressure in Europe, Infantino continues to receive significant backing elsewhere. The Confederation of African Football has publicly supported his leadership, while South American governing body Conmebol has rejected attempts to remove him outside FIFA’s established electoral process.

Infantino traveled to Cali, Colombia, on Friday for the inauguration of newly elected right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella, where Conmebol president Alejandro Domínguez reiterated his support. Domínguez said Infantino’s work at FIFA should not be ignored and called for disagreements within world football to be resolved through dialogue.

The competing statements highlight a widening divide within international football ahead of the 2027 FIFA presidential election. For years, Infantino appeared to be heading toward another term with relatively little resistance. The collapse of the private investment plan and the increasingly public confrontation between FIFA and UEFA have now turned what once looked like a straightforward reelection campaign into one of the most serious leadership crises of his decade in charge.

World.title: Costa Rica Reports Renewed Increase in COVID-19 Cases
World.content:
COVID-19 has once again become the most widely circulating respiratory virus detected in Costa Rica, as health officials urge residents to take basic precautions amid an increase in cases and hospitalizations. The latest epidemiological surveillance places COVID-19 ahead of rhinovirus and parainfluenza among respiratory viruses currently circulating here.

During epidemiological week 29, covering July 13 through July 19, Costa Rica recorded 126 confirmed COVID-19 cases, up from 94 the previous week. That represents an increase of about 34%. Hospitalizations also climbed, with 29 COVID-19 patients receiving hospital care compared with 18 the previous week, an increase of roughly 56%. Five deaths associated with COVID-19 were reported during the same epidemiological week.

The figures remain far below the levels Costa Rica experienced during the height of the pandemic, and there is currently no national health alert for respiratory illnesses. However, the change in circulation has prompted renewed attention as several respiratory viruses spread simultaneously.

Costa Rica has recorded more than 771,000 cases of respiratory illness so far this year, a broader figure that includes illnesses caused by multiple viruses rather than COVID-19 alone. Children, older adults and people with chronic health conditions remain among those considered most vulnerable to complications from respiratory infections.

Health authorities are recommending many of the familiar measures used to reduce respiratory infections: keeping vaccinations current, washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes and choosing well-ventilated spaces when possible. People experiencing respiratory symptoms are also being encouraged to avoid crowded activities and limit close contact with vulnerable relatives or friends until they recover.

The renewed circulation of COVID-19 comes during Costa Rica’s rainy season, when respiratory illnesses can become more noticeable as people spend more time indoors and several viruses circulate at the same time. For residents and travelers, the latest numbers do not signal a return to pandemic-era restrictions. There have been no announcements of renewed mask mandates, travel requirements or widespread restrictions connected to the current increase.

Instead, the emphasis remains on individual precautions, particularly for people at greater risk of serious illness. Health officials continue to monitor COVID-19 alongside influenza, rhinovirus, parainfluenza and other respiratory illnesses to identify changes in circulation and hospital demand.

World.title: Gunmen Storm Costa Rica Hospital and Kill Patient in Nicoya
World.content:
Two masked gunmen forced their way into a public hospital in Guanacaste early Saturday and shot a patient to death as he lay on a stretcher in the observation area, in an unusually brazen attack that has prompted tighter security at the facility. The shooting occurred between approximately 3:05 a.m. and 3:10 a.m. at Hospital La Anexión in Nicoya.

The attackers arrived by car carrying long guns believed to be AR-15-style rifles. They threatened a hospital security guard, entered the building and went directly to the area where the patient was being treated. The victim, identified by the surnames Valverde Matarrita, was 32 years old. He was shot multiple times in the face and chest and died at the hospital.

Valverde Matarrita had been admitted approximately two days earlier for an injury to one of his legs and remained under observation when the gunmen entered the facility. An elderly woman was also struck by gunfire during the attack. She suffered a gunshot wound to the buttock but was reported in stable condition, and the injury was not considered life-threatening.

Authorities have since revealed that Valverde Matarrita previously had police protection ordered by prosecutors in Guanacaste. That protection, however, had been withdrawn before Saturday’s attack. Officials have not yet explained publicly why the protection was removed or why the victim may have been targeted.

Police started an operation to locate the attackers following the shooting. The car used in the escape has been found by authorities, but no arrests had been announced as of Saturday afternoon. The Judicial Investigation Agency, known as the OIJ, is investigating the killing. The Costa Rican Social Security Fund, which operates the public hospitals, reinforced security at Hospital La Anexión following the attack. Hospital services continued operating normally Saturday.

The shooting is particularly brazen because the attackers were willing to enter an operating medical facility, threaten security personnel and move through the hospital to reach their intended target. Hospital La Anexión is one of the main public medical centers serving Nicoya and surrounding communities on the Nicoya Peninsula, including an area heavily visited by foreign tourists and home to a sizable expatriate population.

The attack adds another security concern for Guanacaste, where authorities have been confronting violent crime linked to disputes between criminal groups in parts of the province. For the hospital, the immediate issue is how two heavily armed men were able to get inside the facility and reach a patient. Security has already been strengthened while investigators work to reconstruct the attack and identify those responsible.

No motive for the killing had been announced by Saturday afternoon.

World.title: Lionel Messi’s Father Jorge Messi Dies After Long Illness
World.content:
Jorge Messi, the father and longtime representative of Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi, has died at age 68 following a prolonged illness. Jorge Messi died early Saturday at a medical clinic in Rosario, Argentina, where he had been receiving treatment. The specific illness and medical cause of death have not been made public at the family’s request.

Lionel Messi is expected to travel from Miami to Rosario to be with his family and attend a private wake. The 39-year-old Argentina captain had spent time with his father following the 2026 World Cup before returning to Inter Miami. Jorge Messi was far more than the father of one of soccer’s greatest players. He played a central role in Lionel Messi’s career from his earliest years in Rosario and later handled many of the business and contractual decisions surrounding his son.

When Messi was a young player at Newell’s Old Boys and required treatment for a growth hormone deficiency, Jorge helped search for a club capable of supporting both his development and medical needs. That search eventually led the family to Barcelona when Messi was 13 years old. Jorge remained in Spain with his son during a difficult adjustment period, helping set the foundation for the career that followed.

Messi would eventually spend more than two decades connected to Barcelona, becoming the club’s all-time leading scorer and winning numerous domestic and European titles before moving to Paris Saint-Germain in 2021 and Inter Miami in 2023. Jorge continued to serve as a key adviser and representative throughout those moves and remained closely involved in his son’s professional career.

Concerns about his health became public during the 2026 World Cup in North America. Lionel Messi became emotional after scoring during Argentina’s opening match against Algeria and later said he had been dealing with difficult circumstances away from soccer. Days later, the Messi family confirmed that Jorge was undergoing medical treatment while asking for privacy. The family had also pushed back strongly against premature reports at the time claiming he had died.

Saturday’s confirmed death prompted tributes throughout the soccer world. The Argentine Football Association ordered a minute of silence at matches across the country, with players, coaches and referees wearing black armbands. Flags at AFA facilities were also lowered to half-staff.

Newell’s Old Boys, where Lionel Messi began playing as a child, remembered Jorge as a central figure behind his son’s career. Barcelona also paid tribute to him, recognizing the trust he placed in the club when Lionel arrived as a teenager. Real Madrid and other clubs and organizations also sent condolences to the Messi family.

Jorge is survived by his wife, Celia Cuccittini, and their four children, Rodrigo, Matías, Lionel and María Sol. For Lionel Messi, the loss comes just weeks after Argentina completed another World Cup run and as he returned to club competition with Inter Miami. His club was scheduled to face Monterrey in the Leagues Cup on Saturday night.

World.title: Why the Cincinnati Open Is the Last Major Test Before the US Open
World.content:
The Cincinnati Open begins opening its grounds to fans this weekend, but for the players arriving in Mason, Ohio, the tournament carries considerably more weight than another stop on the summer schedule. Cincinnati is the final ATP Masters 1000 and WTA 1000 tournament before the US Open, making the next two weeks one of the clearest tests of who is ready to contend in New York and who still has work to do.



Qualifying begins August 11 at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, followed by the men’s and women’s main draws on August 13. The Cincinnati singles finals will be played August 23. Exactly one week later, on August 30, the US Open singles main draws begin in New York. That short turnaround is what gives Cincinnati its importance.

Players who make deep runs will arrive at Flushing Meadows with confidence, match fitness and proof that their games are working on North American hard courts. Those struggling with injuries, form or the transition from other surfaces have little time left to make adjustments.

Cincinnati Offers a Grand Slam-Level Test

Cincinnati is not a Grand Slam, but the quality of competition makes it one of the closest things players will encounter before New York. The men’s tournament is an ATP Masters 1000 event and the women’s competition carries WTA 1000 status. Both feature 96-player singles draws filled with many of the highest-ranked players in the world.

A Masters 1000 title on the men’s side is worth 1,000 ranking points, while the tournament also offers substantial ranking opportunities throughout the draw. But Cincinnati’s value goes beyond points.

Players will face many of the same opponents they could encounter a week later at the US Open, often under demanding summer conditions. Long matches, heat, humidity and repeated days of competition provide a useful indication of who is physically prepared for a two-week Grand Slam.

It also gives players another chance to solve problems that became apparent earlier in the North American hard-court season. A serve that was effective on another surface may not produce the same results. A player struggling to defend a second serve or finish short balls has very little time remaining to correct those weaknesses.

By Cincinnati, experimentation begins to give way to urgency.

Hard Courts Change the Equation

The transition to North American hard courts is particularly important because the US Open rewards a different combination of skills than the European clay and grass seasons that dominate the preceding months. Movement changes. Points can develop more quickly. First serves and returns become increasingly important, and players who can take control of the baseline early are often rewarded.

For players who built much of their season on clay, Cincinnati can provide an especially revealing test. That makes the tournament worth watching closely for Latin American tennis fans. Brazil’s João Fonseca, Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, Sebastián Báez and Tomás Martín Etcheverry, Peru’s Ignacio Buse and Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo are among the players from the region heading into the Cincinnati period with the US Open approaching.

Colombia’s Camila Osorio leads the Latin American presence on the women’s side, with other players from the region attempting to reach the main draw through qualifying. The question for each is not simply how far they can advance in Ohio. Cincinnati will provide another measure of how well their games are translating to the surface they will encounter in New York.

Ranking Points Matter, But So Does the Draw

Cincinnati can also change a player’s position heading into the final Grand Slam of the season. A deep run at a 1000-level tournament can produce a substantial rankings boost, particularly for players clustered closely together in the standings. That matters because rankings help determine seedings and ultimately influence the path a player may face through a major tournament.

For someone near one of those dividing lines, a strong Cincinnati performance can have consequences beyond the tournament itself. The difference between being seeded and unseeded at a Grand Slam can mean avoiding one of the world’s highest-ranked players in the opening rounds.

Even for players whose US Open position is already secure, Cincinnati provides something equally valuable: matches against elite opposition. There is little substitute for facing one of the world’s best players shortly before a Grand Slam.

Fitness Will Be Closely Watched

Cincinnati will also offer important clues about injuries and fatigue. The professional tennis calendar leaves little recovery time during the summer. Players move from Europe to North America and then through a series of hard-court tournaments before reaching New York. Some arrive in Cincinnati searching for matches. Others arrive needing rest. Finding the balance is difficult.

A player eliminated early may lose an opportunity to build match rhythm before the US Open. A player who reaches the Cincinnati final could play through August 23 and then have only seven days before the first Sunday of singles competition in New York. That creates difficult decisions for players dealing with even relatively minor physical problems.

The withdrawal of defending men’s champion Carlos Alcaraz because of a wrist injury is a reminder of how quickly the complexion of the tournament can change at this point in the season. Others will arrive trying to manage their workloads while still pursuing one of the biggest titles available outside the Grand Slams.

What Cincinnati Can Tell Us

Tournament results alone will not predict the US Open. Tennis history is filled with players who struggled in their final warm-up tournament and then found their best form at a Grand Slam. Others have arrived in New York carrying a long winning streak only to lose early.

Still, several things will be worth watching in Cincinnati. How players move after long matches. Whether their first serves remain effective late in sets. How aggressively they return. Whether they can maintain their level through consecutive days of competition. And perhaps most importantly, how comfortable they look.

By the middle of August, there are few opportunities remaining to completely rebuild a game before the US Open. Cincinnati is where many of those questions begin to receive answers. The tournament’s qualifying rounds start August 11, with main-draw play beginning August 13 and the singles finals scheduled for August 23.

The US Open begins its Fan Week and qualifying activities the same day Cincinnati crowns its champions, before the main singles draws start August 30. For tennis fans here in Costa Rica and across Latin America, that makes Cincinnati much more than a warm-up event. It is the last major checkpoint before the tennis world turns its attention to New York.

World.title: Where You Can Fly Nonstop to Costa Rica This High Season
World.content:
Getting to Costa Rica is about to get easier from a lot more places. Fourteen new or expanded nonstop flights start between October and March, and several of them connect cities that have never had a direct flight here. One heavily promoted route has already been cancelled, and it is worth knowing which. If you are planning a trip for the high season, or you have family flying down to visit, this is the list you need.

Every route below is confirmed by the airline, with start dates, days of the week and aircraft where those have been published. The expansion follows a strong year for arrivals. Between January and June, 1,605,360 travelers landed in Costa Rica by air, up 7.8% over the same six months of 2025 and the best first half on record.

New flights to San Jose

Las Vegas is off the table. Southwest announced a daily overnight Las Vegas to San Jose route in February, pushed the launch from October to November, then cancelled it in July before a single flight operated. The airline cited fuel costs and a decision to use its aircraft more efficiently, since an overnight leaves a plane parked in Costa Rica for hours. If you were waiting on that one, stop waiting.

That leaves the western United States where it was. From Nevada, Arizona and most of California you are still connecting through Houston, Miami or another gateway to reach Costa Rica.

Breeze Airways arrives from Tampa on October 3. This is the airline’s first-ever service to Costa Rica and makes the country its fifth international destination. Flights run Wednesdays and Saturdays on an Airbus A220 seating 137. Tampa has not had a direct link to San Jose in more than 25 years.

Air Transat starts Quebec City on December 15, once a week. Unlike most of the winter additions, this one is permanent rather than seasonal, and it brings the number of Canadian cities with direct flights to Costa Rica to seven.

Porter connects Toronto Pearson from December 2 through April 30, four flights a week on an Embraer E195-E2 seating 132. The aircraft has no middle seats.

Southwest adds Austin on March 13, 2027, Saturdays only. It is the only nonstop between Central Texas and San Jose. The outbound leaves Austin at 10:25 a.m. and lands at 2:05 p.m., with the return departing at 3:05 p.m. Tickets are already on sale.

New flights to Guanacaste

Liberia keeps pulling ahead. Daniel Oduber Quiros handled its busiest quarter ever in early 2026, and airlines have noticed. Air Canada flies Vancouver from December 13 through April 12, Mondays and Thursdays on a Boeing 737 MAX 8 seating 177. Canadian traffic through Liberia grew 28% in the first half of this year, which is the main reason so many of these routes point north.

WestJet adds Ottawa from December 20 through April 4, Sundays, on a 737 MAX 8 seating 174. Worth knowing before you shop: Porter already flies Ottawa to Liberia weekly through the winter, so from December you have two nonstop options on that route rather than one.

United flies Washington-Dulles daily from December 17 through January 4. Note how short that window is. It is a holiday-season route, not a winter-long one, and if you want it you should book early. The aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9 with 179 seats including 20 in business.

That route also completes something unusual. United will now serve Liberia from all seven of its US hubs, alongside Newark, Denver, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Houston and Chicago. Delta returns to New York JFK from December 19 through April 10, Saturdays only, on an Airbus A321neo seating 194. Delta last flew this route in 2016, and it currently offers no service at all between New York City and Costa Rica.

Southwest adds Nashville from February 13 to March 6, 2027, Saturdays, on a 737 MAX 8. That is a four-week window, the shortest on this list.

Costa Rica gets its first flights from Poland

The most unexpected addition is a charter series. Rainbow Tours and LOT Polish Airlines will run eleven flights into Liberia on a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner seating 251, the first direct air link between Poland and Costa Rica. Warsaw Chopin operates weekly from October 8 to 29. Katowice takes over weekly from November 5 to December 17.

These are charter operations sold through a tour operator, so you will not find them on a standard flight search. If you have family in Poland planning a visit, that is the booking route.

More Seats from Europe

Three European carriers are adding frequencies rather than new destinations, which matters if you have struggled to find a seat on a specific day.

British Airways moves to Heathrow on October 25 and goes from three to five weekly flights through March, operating Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays on a Boeing 787-8. If you connect onward in Europe, this is the change that matters most. Heathrow is the airline’s main hub, and it has never had scheduled service to Costa Rica or anywhere in Central America until now.

Lufthansa moves from three to five weekly Frankfurt flights from October 25 to March 27, operating Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. The days change as well as the count, so check yours. The route currently runs Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays. Lufthansa is also switching to a Boeing 787-9 with its newer Allegris cabin.

Iberojet adds a third weekly Madrid flight on Thursdays from late November. The airline expects to make it permanent across 2027 and 2028.

The full list

Airline Route Starts Days Southwest Las Vegas to San Jose Cancelled Dropped before launch Breeze Tampa to San Jose Oct 3 Wed, Sat LOT (charter) Warsaw to Liberia Oct 8 to 29 Weekly British Airways London Heathrow to San Jose Oct 25 (3 to 5 weekly) Tue, Wed, Fri, Sat, Sun Lufthansa Frankfurt to San Jose Oct 25 (3 to 5 weekly) Mon, Wed, Fri, Sat, Sun LOT (charter) Katowice to Liberia Nov 5 to Dec 17 Weekly Iberojet Madrid to San Jose Late Nov (2 to 3 weekly) Adds Thu Porter Toronto to San Jose Dec 2 to Apr 30 4 weekly Air Canada Vancouver to Liberia Dec 13 to Apr 12 Mon, Thu Air Transat Quebec City to San Jose Dec 15 Weekly United Washington-Dulles to Liberia Dec 17 to Jan 4 Daily Delta New York JFK to Liberia Dec 19 to Apr 10 Sat WestJet Ottawa to Liberia Dec 20 to Apr 4 Sun Southwest Nashville to Liberia Feb 13 to Mar 6 Sat Southwest Austin to San Jose Mar 13, 2027 Sat

Before you book

Pick your airport before you pick your flight. Liberia puts you within a short drive of Tamarindo, Nosara, Playas del Coco, Papagayo, Flamingo and Santa Teresa. San Jose is better for the Caribbean side, the Central Valley, the southern Pacific and anywhere you need a domestic connection. Landing at the wrong one can add four or five hours of driving to your first day.

Watch the end dates as closely as the start dates. Several of these routes run for weeks rather than months, and a return flight that does not exist yet is a common way to get stuck paying for a connection you did not plan. Liberia also operates only between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m., so late arrivals are not an option there regardless of what a search engine shows you.

Seasonal routes get pulled when they do not sell. If a specific one matters to your plans, booking it early does more than save money, it helps keep the route on the schedule. That is also the argument for travel insurance on a seasonal route. If an airline drops the flight or shifts the schedule after you have booked hotels and tours around it, a policy that covers trip interruption is what stands between you and paying twice.

World.title: Costa Rica Warns Pet Owners After Rabies Kills Cattle in Golfito
World.content:
A rabies outbreak that killed three cattle in southern Costa Rica has prompted renewed warnings for ranchers and pet owners to keep animals vaccinated, particularly in areas where vampire bats can transmit the virus. The latest outbreak was found in Pilón, in the area around Pavones, Golfito. The affected farm was placed under quarantine, and all 165 cattle on the property were ordered vaccinated as part of efforts to prevent further spread.

People who had direct contact with the infected animals are also receiving preventive treatment. The Golfito outbreak brings the number of reported paralytic bovine rabies outbreaks in Costa Rica to five so far in 2026. Cases have been recorded in Upala, Cañas, Osa and Golfito, reinforcing concern in rural areas where cattle and wildlife frequently come into contact.

The virus affecting cattle in these outbreaks is primarily transmitted by vampire bats, particularly Desmodus rotundus, a species that feeds on blood. Infected bats can bite the same animal repeatedly over several nights, allowing the virus to enter the animal’s body if it has not been vaccinated.

For cattle, rabies often appears differently than the aggressive form commonly associated with infected dogs. Bovine cases typically develop what is known as paralytic or “dumb” rabies. Early signs can include weakness in the rear legs, difficulty walking and problems remaining upright. As the disease advances, animals may develop paralysis of the tail and jaw, excessive salivation, difficulty swallowing and eventually become unable to stand.

The disease is fatal once it develops. The concern extends beyond cattle. Veterinary specialists are urging residents in affected and rabies-prone areas to make sure dogs and cats are current on their annual rabies vaccinations. Cats can face particular exposure because they sometimes hunt bats that enter homes, barns or nearby buildings. An unvaccinated dog or cat that contracts rabies can then expose people through bites, scratches or saliva.

Those in the area are also being warned not to handle bats, whether they appear healthy, injured or dead. Anyone bitten by a bat or who believes they may have had direct contact with one should seek medical attention immediately rather than waiting for symptoms to develop. Preventive treatment is most effective when started before the virus reaches the nervous system.

Costa Rica is home to a large diversity of bat species, and the current warning should not be seen as a reason to harm them. Most bats play important roles in the ecosystem by eating insects, spreading seeds and pollinating plants. The concern surrounding bovine rabies is focused primarily on blood-feeding vampire bats and the possibility of infected animals passing the virus to livestock or domestic animals.

Current control efforts emphasize vaccination rather than widespread killing of bats. Livestock in affected areas can be vaccinated, domestic animals kept current on their shots, and suspected cases reported quickly so veterinary teams can investigate. Ranchers are being told to watch cattle closely for neurological symptoms and to avoid handling animals showing unexplained paralysis, excessive salivation, coordination problems or sudden changes in behavior.

Suspected animals should not be moved, and carcasses should not be removed or handled without guidance from animal health personnel. The Golfito outbreak is particularly noteworthy in Costa Rica’s southern area, where cattle farms overlap with extensive forest and wildlife habitat.

Pavones is better known internationally for its beaches and surfing, but much of the surrounding canton remains rural, with farms, forests and small communities spread across a large area. There has been no indication that the outbreak poses a general threat to visitors traveling to Pavones or Golfito. The practical concern is direct contact with infected animals or bats, particularly for ranchers, veterinarians, farm workers and people living with unvaccinated pets in affected areas.

For most people the best protection is to keep dogs, cats and livestock vaccinated and report animals showing unusual neurological symptoms. This new warning comes as Costa Rica balances two important priorities: protecting livestock and public health while recognizing the ecological importance of bats in controlling insects, pollinating plants and dispersing seeds throughout Costa Rica’s ecosystems.

World.title: Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street
World.content:
Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Breaking Belize News has received reports of a serious traffic accident involving motorcycles on Mahogany Street in Belize City during the early hours of Sunday morning.

Preliminary information indicates that the accident occurred at around 2:00 a.m. and involved at least two motorcycles. Images from the scene show multiple persons on the roadway as bystanders and other individuals gathered nearby.

Initial reports indicate that at least one person may have died, while there are also unconfirmed reports suggesting that two persons were killed in the collision.

The identities of those involved and the circumstances leading to the accident have not yet been confirmed.

Breaking Belize News will provide additional information once an official report becomes available.

World.title: Teen drowns in Belize River after bee swarm attack
World.content:
Teen drowns in Belize River after bee swarm attack

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A quiet walk along the Philip Goldson Highway turned to tragedy on Friday, August 7, 2026, when a 17-year-old girl drowned in the Belize River after she and her father were attacked by a swarm of bees near mile 7, sending the teen into deep water from which she never resurfaced.

The attack came at about 1:00 p.m., as the girl and her father, residents of Lord’s Bank who often walked that route together, passed a tree stump where the bees were nesting. The swarm descended on them both, and in the chaos that followed, as passersby rushed to assist her father, the teen went into the river, likely to escape the stings. That stretch of the river is said to be about 20 feet deep, and the girl, who could not swim, was unable to get back to the surface.

What followed was an hours-long search that drew together the Belize Coast Guard and eight civilian volunteers from 501 Lifeguard, who waded and dove through dark, murky water until about 3:30 p.m., when her body was finally recovered.

Tevin Conorquie, the 501 Lifeguard swimming instructor who first located her, described the ordeal, speaking to local media. “All we could have done was free dive and try to scan the area,” he said. “Due to the darkness of the water, it was intense for us to see but we still pulled through, we had the faith and the courage and we did what we had to do.” The team spent some three to four hours in the water, in conditions Conorquie called very difficult, “due to the fact that we know there may be crocodiles with us as well.”

When the teen’s brother arrived and the loss became real, the rescuers’ work turned from search to solace, the 501 Lifeguard team circling him in prayer. “With our team it’s just love,” said the organization’s owner, Andrew Gentle, noting that his instructors left their swimming classes to answer the call, and the whole team came.

The recovery weighed on the professionals too. “It’s never easy because you’re talking about the loss of life,” said Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis, Commandant of the Belize Coast Guard, which responded to the request for dive operations. “There were times when I myself shed tears because of the situation. Especially when you’re talking about a young person such as the one today.”

The girl’s father is currently recovering in hospital. The family shared that the teen was living with autism and resided with her father. Officials have since sprayed the area where the bees were nesting.

Breaking Belize News extends its deepest condolences to the family, and its gratitude to the divers and volunteers who refused to leave the river without her.

World.title: The 80 million dollar question, a ledger for Belizeans to judge the BTL Speednet deal
World.content:
The 80 million dollar question, a ledger for Belizeans to judge the BTL Speednet deal

By Horace Palacio:

This week, the board of Belize Telemedia Limited approved spending 80 million dollars to buy Speednet, the company Belizeans know as Smart. It did so one day after the Chamber of Commerce publicly begged it to halt. The final agreement still must return to the board before signing, which means one thing.

There is still time for you to think. And you must, because this is not somebody else’s transaction.

BTL is majority owned by the Government of Belize, which is to say, by you. The Social Security Board, holding the retirement contributions of every working Belizean, owns another 34.2 percent. When BTL spends 80 million dollars, it is your company spending what is ultimately your money, with your pension fund along for the ride. You are the shareholder here. So today I will not hand you a verdict. I will hand you the ledger, both columns, honestly weighed, and then I will hand you the gavel.

First, the case for the deal, and let me make it properly, because it is not foolish.

Belize is a nation of 420,000 people carrying two complete, parallel telecommunications networks. Two sets of towers climbing the same skyline. Two fiber networks running down the same streets. Two billing systems, two headquarters, two of everything, serving a market smaller than a single foreign city. The case says this duplication is waste a small country cannot afford, and that one consolidated network could finally achieve the scale to modernize seriously, push fiber and coverage into the villages that neither company found profitable to serve, and strengthen reliability nationwide. BTL says the purchase needs no borrowing and not one new dollar from Social Security, paying for itself from Speednet’s own cash flows in roughly 4.2 years, with the profits of a unified telecom flowing to public hands instead of private ones. And there is a quieter argument some will weigh, that this deal ends Lord Ashcroft’s presence in Belizean telecommunications once and for all. That is the case for. Taken at face value, it is a vision of efficiency, inclusion, and sovereignty.

Now the other column, and it is heavy.

Start with what we already lived. Belizeans of a certain age remember the old single-provider era, and what it delivered, some of the region’s most expensive and slowest service, because a customer with nowhere to go is a customer who need not be pleased. Then competition arrived, and in the PUC’s own public comment file on this very deal sits a citizen pointing to the large price gap between BTL and Speednet as exactly what stands to be lost. Competition is not a theory in Belize. It is the reason your phone plan got better. This deal ends it.

Then the law. Section 42(4) of the Telecommunications Act prohibits agreements that significantly lessen competition in telecommunications. Buying your only major competitor is about the purest example imaginable. The Chamber adds a deeper alarm, Belize has no comprehensive competition or merger control legislation at all, no guardrails, meaning this would be a state-backed monopoly overseen only by a regulator, and the Chamber’s blunt warning is that regulation can never truly replace competition. Which raises the question no one has answered. When government owns the only telecom, and government appoints the referee, who exactly protects you?

Then the valuation. The financial model that justified the 80 million figure was prepared by Moore, a firm the unions say holds established ties to the BTL board, and it was paid for by BTL, the buyer, and reports indicate it stands among the only documents board members received. The unions call that a conflict of interest that renders the number inherently suspect, and demand what any buyer of a used car would demand, an independent inspection.

Then the arithmetic itself, because analysts who have studied the projections raise eyebrows at every line. The model reportedly projects Speednet earning a 66.5 percent profit margin, far above BTL’s own 44 percent, on revenue of 69 million dollars. Skeptics who place Speednet’s realistic revenue nearer 28 to 32 million calculate that the payback stretches not to 4.2 years but to somewhere between 13 and 25. The company’s own slides reportedly show combined revenue going flat, growing under one percent yearly once the deal closes, meaning the promised leap in profits rests almost entirely on cutting costs. And the seller’s own press release confirms where the knife lands, power, software, maintenance, and the duplicated departments, sales, marketing, human resources, finance, IT, purchasing. Behind every one of those words sit Belizean employees whose futures nobody has yet disclosed. BTL claims its payback is calculated on a discounted basis, yet the standard tools of any public investment of this size, the net present value, the internal rate of return, the formal schedules, have not been published for the shareholders, meaning you, to see.

Now count the voices, because the scorecard on this deal is unlike anything in recent memory. In favor, the BTL board and management. Urging halt or answers, the Chamber of Commerce speaking for over six thousand employers, the National Trade Union Congress speaking for organized labor, the parliamentary Opposition, and all four independent senators in a joint statement. Stop and appreciate the rarity. The employers and the unions of this country agree with each other about once a decade. They agree on this. When both the boss and the worker smell the same smoke, wise citizens check for fire.

So, Belize, was 80 million dollars for a national telecom monopoly worth it, or not? That verdict belongs to you. But hear me carefully, because this is the entire point of today’s column.

No honest verdict can be rendered on sealed evidence. Before any Belizean, for or against, can truly judge this deal, six things must be put on the table. Speednet’s audited financial statements for the past five years, so the revenue dispute dies on facts. A second, fully independent, internationally credible valuation, so the price stands on neutral ground. The full financial workings, published, so the payback claim can be tested by any accountant in the country. The honest scope of planned redundancies, so workers stop learning their futures from press releases. A public, rigorous PUC merger review under Section 42(4), conducted as law, not formality. And binding, enforceable consumer protections, in writing, before signing, not promises after.

If this deal is as good as its backers insist, none of that sunlight costs them anything. Good deals survive audits. Only bad ones fear them. And a transaction this size, by a publicly owned company, in a country still raw from the Mira Millions lesson about what happens in the dark, must be concluded in daylight or not at all.

The board has voted. The ink is not dry. You are the shareholder, Belize, all 420,000 of you.

Demand the books. Read the ledger. Then judge.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Jorge Messi, father and lifelong architect of Lionel’s career, dies at 68
World.content:
Jorge Messi, father and lifelong architect of Lionel’s career, dies at 68

By Breaking Belize News Staff ( HP): Jorge Messi, the father of Argentina captain Lionel Messi and the man who guided every step of the greatest career in football history, died Saturday at a hospital in Rosario, Argentina. He was 68.

Club Atlético Newell’s Old Boys, the Rosario club where both father and son once played in the youth ranks, announced his death, saying he had undergone treatment in recent months for an unspecified illness. The club described him as “the pillar and the person who, with vision, rigor and affection, supported the career of the best player of all time, alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini.”

The announcement casts the recent World Cup in a new and poignant light. After scoring against Algeria in Argentina’s opening match, Messi was visibly emotional, later saying he wept for “a reason unrelated to sports” and that he had endured “difficult, complicated days.” Media speculation at the time drew a sharp statement from the Messi family confirming that Jorge was experiencing a health issue, while insisting that “a person’s health and the peace of mind of their loved ones should not be the subject of speculation.” Messi went on to captain Argentina to the final, where they finished runners-up to Spain, before returning home to rest.

A chemical technician and former steelworker, Jorge Messi played as a midfielder in Newell’s youth system before military service ended his own football path. His life’s work became his son’s. He traveled with a young Lionel to Barcelona in the early 2000s for the trial that opened La Masia’s doors, negotiated the contracts with Barcelona and the later moves to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami, and managed his son’s business affairs throughout.

Lionel Messi himself once described what those early days cost them both. “Sometimes I would lock myself in my room to cry when we arrived in Barcelona, or my dad would do the same without me seeing him,” he said in 2007. “My dad even asked me what I wanted to do when we were feeling down, if I wanted to stay or go back, and I wanted to stay, and he stayed with me.”

Tributes flowed Saturday. CONMEBOL offered condolences “with respect and affection for Lionel,” and Argentine federation president Claudio Tapia honoured Jorge “for having raised a person of values: humble, respectful, and deeply committed to others.” The federation ordered a moment of silence at all matches across every category of Argentine football, with players, referees and coaching staff to wear black armbands.

Jorge Messi is survived by his wife Celia and their children. Breaking Belize News extends condolences to the Messi family.

World.title: BDF and University of Belize deepen partnership on education and training
World.content:
BDF and University of Belize deepen partnership on education and training

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Defence Force and the University of Belize are strengthening their collaboration, with the BDF’s Training and Doctrine Directorate visiting the university to meet with President and members of his staff on furthering joint efforts between the Ministry of Defence and Border Security and the nation’s leading academic institution.

The engagement provided an opportunity for discussions on ongoing programs, future initiatives, and the continued growth of the partnership between the two institutions, according to the BDF.

Members of the Force also attended the closing ceremony of the Digital Literacy Program hosted by the University of Belize, a program in which the BDF proudly participated. The Force described the training as another important step in equipping its members with valuable knowledge and skills for both professional and personal development.

With the university preparing for the upcoming academic year, plans were established to continue and expand engagements between both institutions.

The BDF said it remains committed to promoting higher learning, professional development and continuous education as essential components in transforming training and developing a more capable and knowledgeable Force, summing up the effort in its own words: investing in education, strengthening our Force, serving Belize.

World.title: Black Orchid Resort gives locals 20 percent off all rooms through October 1
World.content:
Black Orchid Resort gives locals 20 percent off all rooms through October 1

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP):Belizeans looking for a getaway without the border run have a fresh reason to look toward Burrell Boom. Black Orchid Resort has launched its River Wild Escape locals special, offering 20 percent off all rooms for Belizean residents from August 1 to October 1.

The discount applies across the resort’s full range of accommodations: Garden View Rooms, River View Rooms, Garden View Suites and Riverfront Suites, so everything from a simple couple’s night away to a riverfront splurge qualifies.

The package is pitched as more than just a room.
