World.title: Iraqi authorities arrest former Salah Al Din Governor Abu Mazen
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi security forces arrested former Saladin Governor Ahmed Abdullah al-Jubouri, widely known as “Abu Mazen,” in Baghdad on corruption charges, according to official state media reports on Saturday, August 8, 2026.

In a related enforcement action, security personnel subsequently detained prominent businessman Muhammad al-Hajaf, a close associate of al-Jubouri, over allegations of illegally appropriating funds tied to public infrastructure and service contracts across Saladin Governorate.

Key Operational Takeaways

High-Profile Arrests: Former Governor and MP Ahmed al-Jubouri (“Abu Mazen”) detained in Baghdad’s Al-Qadisiyah district alongside associate Muhammad al-Hajaf.

Contract Misappropriation: The ongoing probe centers on the misappropriation of public contract funds and financial irregularities in municipal development projects across Saladin Governorate.

Political Background: Al-Jubouri previously served as Governor of Saladin (2013–2014), Minister of State for Provincial Affairs (2014–2015), and a member of the Iraqi Parliament (2015–2022).

Prior Judicial & International Actions: Al-Jubouri was sanctioned by the U.S. Department of the Treasury in 2019 under the Global Magnitsky Act for official corruption and was subject to a March 2026 domestic arrest warrant following a lawsuit filed by Azem Alliance chief Muthanna al-Samarrai.

The arrest of al-Jubouri—who leads the National Masses Party (Al-Jamahir Al-Wataniya)—marks one of the most high-profile enforcement operations under Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi’s ongoing federal anti-corruption campaign.

Judicial sources indicate that investigations into al-Hajaf’s business entities are examining systemic delays and financial improprieties in municipal infrastructure contracts. Neither al-Jubouri nor al-Hajaf has issued an official statement regarding the charges, as federal prosecutors prepare to submit formal audit findings to the judiciary.

World.title: PM Al-Zaidi and French President Macron discuss economic ties and regional stability
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com)— Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi held a high-level telephone discussion with French President Emmanuel Macron on Saturday, August 8, 2026, focusing on expanding economic partnerships, regional security, and the conclusion of the international coalition’s military mission in Iraq.

According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Media Office, the leaders reviewed bilateral cooperation across economic and investment sectors, highlighting expanding opportunities for French corporations within Iraq’s infrastructure and energy markets. Prime Minister al-Zaidi extended an official invitation to President Macron to visit Baghdad to solidify a long-term economic partnership between the two nations.

Key Takeaways from the High-Level Talks

September 30 Coalition Exit Benchmark: Prime Minister al-Zaidi reiterated that September 30, 2026, serves as the definitive deadline for the withdrawal of international coalition military forces from Iraq, noting that concluding the mission allows Baghdad to focus completely on economic development.

Sovereignty & Regional Stability: Al-Zaidi stressed Iraq’s commitment to balanced regional diplomacy, asserting that Iraqi territory will not be utilized to threaten neighboring states, while calling for dialogue to resolve ongoing Middle East conflicts.

French Corporate Investment: The discussions highlighted expanding trade and investment channels for French enterprises across national energy, logistics, and infrastructure sectors.

French Support for Governance Reforms: President Macron reaffirmed France’s commitment to supporting Iraq’s anti-corruption initiatives, fiscal reforms, counter-terrorism cooperation, and security force capacity building.

Prime Minister al-Zaidi emphasized during the call that his administration is focused on transforming Iraq into an influential economic hub linking global trade routes, backed by the country’s strategic location and natural resources.

President Macron praised the Iraqi government’s structural economic reforms and confirmed Paris’s continued support for Iraq’s institutional stability and military modernization as the transition toward a purely bilateral security relationship nears completion.

World.title: Iraq oil exports drop 75% amid Hormuz closure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Oil Minister Hayan Abdul-Ghani announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, that the nation’s crude oil exports have plummeted by 75% due to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and regional military escalations. The severe drop in oil revenues has triggered a liquidity squeeze across the federal government, causing widespread delays in state employee salary disbursements.

Speaking at a press conference in Baghdad, Abdul-Ghani revealed that Iraq is currently exporting only a quarter of its pre-war volumes, which stood at approximately 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) prior to the outbreak of regional hostilities on February 28. He noted that while Baghdad has engaged in diplomatic talks with Iran to permit the passage of Iraqi oil shipments through the Gulf, no operational agreement has been activated.

Key financial and operational highlights

Export Collapse: Iraq’s crude exports have fallen to ~25% of pre-war capacity, cutting off the primary source of state revenue.

Fiscal Pressure & Salary Delays: Reduced export volumes and below-budget sale prices have caused acute liquidity shortages, delaying public sector payrolls.

Corporate Damage Compensation: Domestic Attacks: Baghdad has agreed to compensate foreign energy companies for damages resulting from attacks originating inside Iraqi territory. External Strikes: The government declared itself legally exempt from compensating firms for damages caused by foreign strikes or broader military actions beyond state control.

Alternative Export Bypasses: Baghdad is fast-tracking pipeline infrastructure projects bypassing the Persian Gulf, including routes south toward Turkey’s Ceyhan port, Syria’s Baniyas terminal, and Jordan’s Aqaba port.

To maintain minimal cash flows, Iraq is currently forced to sell its crude at deep price concessions below the baseline benchmark set in the national budget, compounding treasury deficits.

In response to the prolonged maritime chokehold in the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministry of Oil is accelerating infrastructure development along overland export routes.

Priority has been placed on expanding and constructing pipeline corridors connecting southern production hubs to the Mediterranean via Syria and Turkey, alongside long-term transit planning toward the Red Sea via Jordan.

World.title: Iraq activates Kirkuk oil field development contract with BP
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, the official activation of its Kirkuk oilfield development contract with British energy giant BP. The project aims to elevate crude oil production from its current capacity of 320,000 barrels per day (bpd) to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Ministry of Oil Spokesperson Salim Al-Rikabi stated that the contract—initially signed in September 2025—focuses on expanding crude extraction while capturing associated natural gas to eliminate routine flaring and feed domestic power generation infrastructure.

Key operational targets & metrics

Crude Oil Output: Increasing current production from 320,000 bpd to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Associated Gas Capture: Raising associated gas processing from 255 million standard cubic feet per day (scf/d) to a peak capacity of 400 million scf/d.

Facility Modernization: Upgrading and expanding infrastructure across North Oil Company fields and North Gas Company processing plants.

Power & Social Infrastructure: Constructing a dedicated 400-megawatt (MW) power plant, expanding local employment, funding community development initiatives, and upskilling North Oil and North Gas workforces.

Environmental Impact: Phasing out continuous gas flaring to redirect captured methane directly into national electricity generation.

The activation of the Kirkuk project represents a major component of Iraq’s broader energy strategy to achieve natural gas self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on imported fuel.

By upgrading processing facilities managed by the North Gas Company and constructing a dedicated 400 MW power generation facility, the initiative directly addresses regional electricity shortages while reducing environmental emissions.

The partnership also reinforces BP’s operational footprint in northern Iraq, complementing its long-standing management of the Southern Rumaila field and bolstering state-led efforts to modernize national energy infrastructure.

World.title: India’s Reliance pays record $25 million freight cost for Iraqi crude amid Hormuz crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — India’s Reliance Industries (RELI.NS), operator of the world’s largest refining complex in Gujarat, paid an unprecedented record charter fee of $23 million to $25 million for a Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) to transport 2 million barrels of Basrah crude from Iraq, according to shipping sources cited by Reuters on Friday, August 7, 2026.

The extreme freight surge—marking a jump from a pre-war average of $2 million to 12 times the baseline global freight rate—highlights severe shipping chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Daily vessel transits through the strategic waterway have plummeted from a pre-war average of 125–140 ships to a fraction of normal capacity as shipowners avoid military risks.

Key financial & logistics metrics

Soaring Freight Rates: Reliance chartered the VLCC from South Korea’s Sinokor at 1,200 points on the Worldscale freight index—12 times the reference benchmark—up from pre-war levels of 0.8 to 0.9 times ($2 million total).

Deep SOMO Discounts: To offset soaring shipping costs and attract buyers into the Gulf, the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) offered steep discounts of $25 to $30 per barrel below Dubai regional benchmarks.

Net Margin Offset: Despite the $25 million freight tag, energy analysts estimate Reliance will still save millions on the overall transaction due to Iraq’s heavy crude price reductions.

Limited Carrier Pool: Sinokor remains one of the few international maritime operators willing to navigate the Strait of Hormuz to load cargo at Iraq’s Basra Oil Terminal.

While Asian refiners—particularly across India and China—are actively seeking chartered tankers to capture Iraq’s discounted crude allocations, shipowner reluctance continues to limit available tonnage entering the Gulf.

By offering deep price concessions, Iraq’s oil marketing arm is successfully maintaining crude flow off the Basra coast despite soaring war-risk insurance premiums and maritime transport bottlenecks.

World.title: Kata’ib Sayyid Al Shuhada clarifies delay in retaliatory strikes against U.S.-Saudi targets
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Abu Ala al-Walai, Secretary-General of Kata’ib Sayyid al-Shuhada, commented on Saturday, August 8, 2026, regarding the decision by the “Islamic Resistance in Iraq” to pause planned military responses to recent joint U.S.-Saudi strikes.

Speaking via a statement on social media platform X, al-Walai confirmed that the delay was granted at the direct request of Coordination Framework leaders, led by Badr Organization chief Hadi al-Amiri, alongside several independent political figures. However, the paramilitary commander emphasized that options for retaliation—including the reassessment of its timing, scale, and nature—remain fully on the table. He urged state officials to utilize this temporary window to secure Iraq’s rights through diplomatic and legal channels.

Key developments in the escalation pause

The Deferred Response: The Islamic Resistance in Iraq announced on Friday, August 7, the postponement of retaliatory operations originally scheduled for the 23rd of Safar targeting Saudi Arabia and U.S. military bases.

Al-Amiri’s Appeal: Badr Organization leader Hadi al-Amiri issued an urgent video address early Friday urging armed factions to delay military action following American-Saudi strikes on Iraqi territory, prioritizing national stability while pursuing accountability for casualties via diplomatic means.

High Security Readiness: The political appeal followed a volatile night across Baghdad and multiple governorates, prompting high-level security alerts and military deployments across the capital.

Command Structure On Site: In response to directives from Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi to elevate combat readiness, senior commanders from Baghdad Operations Command were deployed on the ground to enforce military discipline and secure vital sectors.

The brief pause in military operations provides a critical window for Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s administration to manage state security, navigate delicate diplomatic channels with Washington and Riyadh, and prevent further regional escalation.

World.title: Iraq fish deaths: 7 alarming signs of a deepening water and pollution crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Recurring Iraq fish deaths are becoming an increasingly serious environmental and economic warning, with the Green Iraq Observatory describing the phenomenon as an annual pattern that reflects the accumulation of two interconnected crises: worsening water scarcity and persistent pollution.

Rather than representing isolated incidents caused by temporary changes in river conditions, the repeated deaths of large numbers of fish across Iraq’s rivers, canals and marshlands suggest that the country’s aquatic ecosystems are coming under sustained pressure from declining water flows, untreated wastewater, industrial pollution and weaknesses in water management.

The latest incidents, recorded in April and August 2026, have once again raised concerns about the condition of Iraq’s freshwater resources and the government’s ability to protect them. According to the observatory, more than 1,000 tonnes of fish died in the Tigris and Diyala rivers during April, with particularly heavy losses reported in Wasit province, while a separate incident occurred earlier this month in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan.

Although the two incidents were associated with different immediate circumstances, they demonstrate how vulnerable Iraq’s aquatic ecosystems have become when declining water levels interact with pollution and inadequate environmental controls.

Iraq fish deaths are becoming an annual warning sign

The Green Iraq Observatory argues that the recurrence of mass fish deaths should no longer be treated as a series of unrelated environmental emergencies. According to its assessment, similar incidents have occurred repeatedly across different parts of Iraq over the past several years, yet the underlying causes have not been addressed with sufficient consistency to prevent them from returning.

This pattern is particularly concerning because rivers and wetlands are not only ecological assets; they also support fisheries, agriculture and the livelihoods of communities that depend directly on healthy waterways.

The observatory said the April incident involved more than 1,000 tonnes of dead fish in the Tigris and Diyala rivers, with the largest losses concentrated in Wasit. It attributed the event to severe contamination caused by untreated sewage and industrial waste, while also pointing to increased water releases from Hamrin Dam that reportedly moved accumulated pollutants downstream toward the Tigris.

The organization further said that more than 20 people experienced poisoning or skin-related injuries and were taken to hospital, illustrating how deterioration in water quality can potentially extend beyond damage to aquatic life and become a broader public-health concern.

A second incident was reported at the beginning of August in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan. According to the observatory, the agriculture and water committee of the Maysan Provincial Council attributed the fish deaths to a sharp decline in the water releases allocated to the canal.

This episode is significant because it demonstrates that pollution is not necessarily the only immediate trigger for fish mortality; inadequate water flows can also create conditions in which fish become increasingly vulnerable to high temperatures, reduced oxygen levels and the concentration of pollutants already present in the water.

Water scarcity Is only part of the problem

Iraq’s water crisis is frequently discussed in terms of declining river flows, prolonged drought and reductions in water arriving from upstream countries. Those factors are undoubtedly important, but the recent fish deaths suggest that the country’s environmental problems cannot be explained simply by saying that Iraq does not have enough water. The quality, distribution and management of the water available can be just as important as its overall volume.

The Green Iraq Observatory highlighted this distinction by noting that the country’s total water storage had reportedly risen to around 34 billion cubic meters at the time of the latest incident.

From the organization’s perspective, the fact that fish mortality continued despite an increase in total reserves indicates that administrative decisions concerning water distribution may be contributing to the problem alongside genuine resource scarcity.

This does not mean that Iraq’s wider water shortage is unimportant. On the contrary, prolonged drought and declining inflows can weaken the natural ability of rivers and wetlands to dilute pollutants and maintain ecological balance. However, when available water is distributed unevenly or when polluted water is allowed to enter already stressed waterways, the consequences can become significantly more severe.

In other words, the crisis is not simply about how much water Iraq has, but also about where the water goes, what quality it has and how effectively it is managed.

Pollution can turn a water shortage into an ecological emergency

Untreated sewage and industrial waste are among the most serious threats facing Iraq’s waterways because they can fundamentally alter the chemical and biological conditions required for aquatic life. When large quantities of organic material enter a river or canal, microorganisms consume oxygen while breaking that material down, potentially reducing dissolved oxygen to levels that fish and other aquatic organisms cannot tolerate.

The situation can become even more complicated when water temperatures rise or when algae proliferate excessively. Some forms of harmful algae can contribute to oxygen depletion, particularly when large quantities of organic matter subsequently decompose.

At the same time, reduced water flows can prevent pollutants from being dispersed naturally, leaving them concentrated in particular sections of a river, canal or wetland.

This combination of factors helps explain why pollution and water scarcity should not be treated as completely separate problems. A waterway with strong flows may have a greater capacity to dilute certain pollutants, whereas a shallow and poorly circulated waterway can become significantly more vulnerable to contamination.

Consequently, environmental protection requires both adequate water releases and strict control over what is discharged into the country’s rivers.

Iraq has experienced similar fish mortality events for years

The latest incidents are not without precedent. The Green Iraq Observatory cited a long record of mass fish mortality events in Iraq, including a major incident in the Euphrates in Babylon in 2018, when tens of thousands of tonnes of fish were reportedly affected.

This was followed by the death of millions of fish at the Hindiya Barrage and another major incident in Al-Dalm Marsh in Diwaniyah in 2020.

Further incidents were reported in the Al-Ezz River in Maysan in 2023, while extensive fish deaths occurred in Ibn Najm Marsh in Najaf last year. Particularly worrying is the recurrence of fish mortality in the Maysan area where a similar incident had already been recorded, because repeated events in the same geographic location can indicate that the environmental conditions responsible for the original problem have not been adequately corrected.

The observatory argues that the repeated nature of these incidents is difficult to reconcile with a system that relies primarily on temporary investigative committees after environmental damage has already occurred. Investigations can establish causes and responsibility, but they cannot substitute for permanent monitoring mechanisms capable of identifying dangerous changes in water quality before they result in large-scale ecological losses.

Iraq’s Marshlands face particular risks

The Iraqi marshlands are especially sensitive to changes in water availability and quality because their ecological health depends on a delicate relationship between water flows, seasonal conditions and the surrounding environment. These wetlands provide habitat for fish and birds while supporting communities whose economic and cultural lives have developed around them over generations.

When water levels fall sharply, sections of the marshes can become isolated or excessively shallow, increasing temperatures and reducing oxygen circulation. If polluted water enters these already stressed environments, the damage can become significantly more difficult to reverse.

Protecting Iraq’s marshlands therefore requires a long-term approach that connects water policy with environmental policy. Maintaining adequate ecological flows, reducing pollution and establishing continuous monitoring systems would be far more effective than treating each fish mortality event as an isolated emergency.

What Iraq can do to prevent future fish deaths

The Green Iraq Observatory has called for several measures aimed at addressing the structural causes behind recurring fish mortality. Among its recommendations is the establishment of fair and sustainable water allocations for provinces and marshlands, rather than relying on short-term decisions that may leave some waterways dangerously depleted.

The observatory has also called for stronger environmental oversight of wastewater treatment facilities and industrial establishments located near rivers. Effective enforcement would require more than regulations on paper; authorities would need regular inspections, reliable water-quality testing and meaningful consequences for facilities that discharge untreated or inadequately treated waste.

Another important proposal is the creation of an early-warning system that monitors dissolved oxygen and pollution levels. Such a system could bring together government agencies, universities and civil-society organizations, allowing scientific data to be collected continuously and shared quickly when dangerous changes are detected.

Finally, rapid compensation for fish farmers affected by major environmental incidents could provide essential economic relief while investigations determine responsibility and long-term solutions.

No. Water scarcity is an important contributing factor, but pollution and poor water management can also play major roles. Even when overall water reserves increase, individual rivers, canals or marshes may experience insufficient flows or deteriorating water quality.

World.title: US Fed sends $500 million cash shipment to Iraq amid financial pressures
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The United States Federal Reserve has sent a new $500 million cash cargo to the Central Bank of Iraq, providing additional dollar liquidity as Baghdad grapples with rising financial pressures and disruptions to its oil-dependent economy.

The shipment was announced by Iraq’s national news agency, citing an official source who claimed the dollars will be used for permitted overseas transfers and transactions involving Iraqi citizens.

Further supplies are planned each month, with a government official estimating annual cash delivery of $8 billion to $10 billion.

These cash payments are part of Iraq’s peculiar financial relationship with the United States.

Proceeds from Iraqi oil exports are mostly placed in an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, with Baghdad obtaining dollars via permitted transfers and cash shipments administered by the Central Bank of Iraq.

The new supply comes at a critical moment for Iraq’s budget.

The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has increased pressure on a nation that relies significantly on oil exports to support government expenditures and get foreign currency.

Iraq’s enormous public-sector pay bill contributes to this vulnerability.

Millions of Iraqis rely directly or indirectly on government wages, pensions, and social benefits; therefore, stable oil income and liquidity are crucial to the national budget.

Baghdad has lately expressed increased worries about its capacity to fulfill expenditure obligations if oil earnings continue low, strengthening long-standing demands for Iraq to diversify government income and lessen its reliance on petroleum exports.

The most recent dollar cargo should offer further liquidity to Iraq’s banking system, but it also shows the country’s vulnerability to both oil-market shocks and its financial ties with Washington at a time of rising regional tensions.

World.title: The women who paint Jharkhand: Sohrai-Khovar's journey from harvest ritual to global gallery
World.content:
A local artisan crouches by her doorstep, her hands stained with mud and colour drawn straight from the earth around her. The warmth of rust red, the hush of chalky white, the depth of a black gone nearly charcoal.

With nothing more than a broken comb and a steady hand, she draws a peacock on a wall still damp from its coating of clay. In a few hours, this wall, like thousands of others across Hazaribagh, will carry the story of the land of Jharkhand, a mural to its beauty.

Sohrai and Khovar paintings are a unique and tribal style of art originating from caves of Jharkhand. In 1991, celebrated and renowned environmentalist Bulu Imam documented rock shelters in the Isco hills of Hazaribagh district and noticed that the motifs on the ancient cave walls closely resembled the paintings still being made on village homes nearby

Imam was able to sketch out a connection between the 21st century walls of a home to the Mesolithic and Chalcolithic caves of 10,000 to 5,000 BCE.

Other researchers, citing the Archaeological Survey of India, place the rock art closer to 7,000-4,000 BCE, in the Paleolithic period.

The dates might be contested but what remains true is that Sohrai and Khovar painting represent one of the longest continuously practiced visual art traditions on the subcontinent, a line running from cave wall to mud wall across several thousand years.

What is Sohrai-Khovar?

Ganju Sohrai painted house (Source: TWAC)

Sohrai was originally a season specific craft style painted around the harvest festival of the same name, celebrated after Diwali in the month of Kartik, when households give thanks to their cattle and to the land.





Inside of a Khovar room (Source: TWAC)

Khovar, the word draws from "kho," meaning cave, and "var," meaning groom, is painted for weddings, decorating the room where a newly married couple will spend their first nights together.

Both styles of art are made almost exclusively by women. Even its heritage tracing follows matrilineal succession, passed down from mothers to daughters. Traditionally it is classified as a Ma-Beti Parampara, with techniques passed down orally rather than written down.

From mud walls to airport terminals

Sanjeev Kumar (IFS), principal chief conservator of forests and head of forest force for Jharkhand, has spent much of his career working alongside these villages. He offers a structural explanation for why this art form became a livelihood tool in the first place, rather than staying purely ceremonial.

Jharkhand's rural economy runs largely on two crop cycles a year, he points out, which leaves long stretches when women in farming households have little steady work.

Between the sowing and the harvest, there is a kind of enforced pause â and in that pause, an entire category of household income simply goes quiet.

Painting, once confined strictly to festival and wedding seasons, has increasingly moved to fill exactly that gap, giving women a way to keep earning in the months the land itself has nothing to offer.

It isn't only about income, in Kumar's telling. Starting in 2007, as Divisional Forest Officer in Dhanbad, he began organising folk art camps to give Sohrai a wider audience, drawing participants from across India and as far as Australia and Bangladesh.

The camps followed him through later postings â Jamshedpur, Hazaribagh, and beyond â running until the pandemic forced them online, then resuming after. The same women who might once have sat out the off-season are now, through this ecosystem, training relatives, negotiating with buyers, and travelling to exhibitions.

Kumar also frames the work as central to the state's eco-tourism ambitions.

Sohrai-Khovar finally received Geographical Indication status in May 2020, reportedly approved in under nine months, unusually fast for a process that typically takes two to three years.

The tag, granted by the Geographical Indication Registry in Chennai, formally recognises the art as unique to the Hazaribagh region, and gave it a marketing foothold it hadn't had before.

The state took the recognition further. Hazaribagh became the first district in Jharkhand to commit to painting all its government buildings with Sohrai motifs â the chief minister's residence, the state secretariat, Ranchi's Birsa Munda Airport, railway stations across Ranchi, Dhanbad, Bokaro, and Tata Nagar all now carry the same red-black-white language once found only on village walls. The art has travelled further still: Prime Minister

is reported to have gifted a Sohrai painting to President Putin, a livelihood project turned, however briefly, into an instrument of diplomacy.

Painting gifted to Russian President Putin by PM Modi

That visibility has translated into real, traceable livelihoods, in at least some cases. Local organisers connecting artists to buyers report dozens of women directly employed through their networks, hundreds more earning supplemental income in season. Cooperatives built specifically to give village women an alternative to farm labour have carried this work to dozens of international exhibitions across Europe and the US, and increasingly Canada, South Africa, and Japan.

Trusts have gone further still â training programmes, small museums, free pigment, and the paperwork that eventually secured the GI tag itself.

Tensions surrounding the craft

Not everyone close to this history agrees the shift toward livelihood has been a clean win. Gustav Imam draws a distinction between his father's original vision and the state's current one. Bulu Imam treated Sohrai as fine art from the start â building an exhibition circuit that ran shows in Australia and Europe.

The government's livelihood framing, Gustav argues, risks something narrower: pay an artist per piece for a product and you've quietly converted her into daily-wage labour rather than treating her as an artist.

He isn't against commercialisation itself; he simply thinks dignity has to come first, and that dignity requires recognition at the very top of the field, not just income at the bottom. Traditions like Madhubani, Warli, and Gond painting have each produced nationally awarded artists, Padma Shri recipients among them; Sohrai-Khovar has not, despite women keeping the tradition alive through real struggle and real limitation.

Until a handful of individual artists receive that kind of recognition, he argues, younger painters have no one concrete to aspire to become.

Gangwa's Lotus - archival art (Source: TWAC)

He also offers a blunt estimate on the schemes meant to help: of the artisans meant to benefit from government portals and initiatives like Mudra loans, perhaps 5 to 10 percent actually do, largely because many are semi-literate and simply can't navigate the registration process.

The rest, in his account, remain outside the system entirely, not excluded by design, but by a bureaucracy that was never built with them in mind.

Coal mining is often folded into this story as a single, simple threat, but the picture splits in two once you look closely. The Isco rock art site itself, the discovery that started everything, has not been destroyed. Dust from nearby mines has crept close and settled on it, but the site was declared a national monument around 2023.

Other rock art caves in the region, more than a dozen now identified, remain safe largely because, in his words, no one knows about them, obscurity standing in for conservation.

Pashupati by Kunti Devi (Source: TWAC)

The villages are a different story. The North Karanpura coalfield sits beneath a large number of tribal villages across Hazaribagh, Ramgarh, and Chatra, and coal projects in the area have displaced multiple villages over the years, acquiring significant stretches of agricultural land in the process.

Residents who've lost land describe rebuilding elsewhere, often some distance from where their families had always lived; local activists warn that further mining could displace still more.

Bulu Imam's decades of opposition â intellectual rather than confrontational, built on letters to officials rather than protest, work that earned him the Gandhi International Peace Award in 2012 â was never really about the rock art surviving.

It was about whether the people who kept painting around it would get to stay.

There is another complication that has nothing to do with mining. Since 2018â19, a central housing scheme, the Pradhan Mantri Gramin Awas Yojana, has replaced mud-and-thatch homes across rural India with brick and cement â a genuine welfare improvement. But Sohrai and Khovar are painted on mud, and the same pigments don't take to cement the same way.

One arm of government is quietly removing the canvas that another arm is simultaneously celebrating, not through malice, but through two policies that were never built with each other in mind.

A seat at the table for indigenous art

The most important complication was hinted at earlier. The market for Sohrai-Khovar remains thin, prices stay low relative to the labour involved, and no fixed floor price exists to stop buyers from talking artists down. Imam suggests that the district administration consider setting a standard pricing for the art to battle some aspects of the issue.

The proposed fix, in Gustav's telling, isn't more schemes. It's status. He points to what happens when a piece lands somewhere with real institutional weight â a Sohrai painting, sold to the American ambassador during a visit to Kolkata, now hangs in a prominent hall at the US consulate.

Contemporary Indian art by named painters routinely sells for crores; indigenous art too deserves a seat at that table. A tradition this old survives not just on income, but on being taken seriously by the people who could otherwise walk past it without a second look.

Exhibition in Rome, 2008 (TWAC)

The artisan finishes her peacock as the light starts to fade. Somewhere else in Hazaribagh, another woman is doing the same. Her red may no longer come from soil gathered by hand, but from a tube of paint bought at the market. The image on the wall is still recognisably Sohrai.

For thousands of years, the art has adapted to changing walls, changing materials and changing lives. But preserving it may require more than putting its motifs on government buildings or selling its paintings to new markets.

It may mean preserving the women who make it, the homes they paint and the communities that taught them how.

The paintings began on cave walls, moved to mud homes and have now travelled to airports, exhibitions and diplomatic gifts. What happens next will depend on whether Sohrai-Khovar is treated simply as a product to be sold â or as a living tradition whose value lies in the people who keep painting it.

World.title: Turbulence-hit AI flight captain screening dope test 'not negative, sent for confirmatory test:' Govt
World.content:
An Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi, experienced a sudden loss of altitude of about 300 feet during cruise

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The pilots of Air Indiaâs Aug 4 turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight were subjected to psychoactive substance (dope) screening test on arrival at the destination. The pilot-in-command or captainâs screening test report was not negative and has been sent for confirmatory tests, the aviation ministry said on Sunday. The ministry has classified the incident as a serious one which will now be probed by Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB). âFurther action, as appropriate, will be taken based on the outcome of the investigation and confirmatory test results,â govt said.Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) rules stipulate that âin case the screening test is non-negative, the employee shall be immediately removed from the safety sensitive duty till a confirmatory report is received. In case of positive confirmatory test for the first time, the concerned employee shall be referred by the organisationâ for de-addiction.The aviation ministry on Sunday said: âOn Aug 4, Air India A320 (VT-EXO), operating flight AI 2379 from Phuket to Delhi, experienced a sudden loss of altitude of about 300 feet during cruise, following which the aircraft stabilised and subsequently landed safely at Delhi. During the occurrence, injuries were reported to a few passengers and cabin crew members on board.The aircraft was carrying 137 passengers, including three infants, and eight crew members comprising two pilots and six cabin crew. ââAs standard operating procedures following such an occurrence, both flight crew members underwent the prescribed psychoactive substance screening test. The screening test in respect of the pilot-in-command (PIC) indicated a result requiring confirmatory testing. Samples have accordingly been sent to the designated laboratory for confirmatory analysis, and the final report is awaited,â it added.Pending investigation, both pilots have been taken off flying duty by the DGCA. âThe aviation ministry and DGCA remain firmly committed to maintaining the highest standards of aviation safety and ensuring that all such occurrences are thoroughly investigated and appropriate action is taken in accordance with the prescribed regulations and procedures,â the statement added.The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet. On arrival in Delhi, 13 passengers and four crew members were hospitalised. People in the know say authorities are probing this case from all angles including whether the handling of this turbulence event was correct; whether the event happened due to weather or some other reason; the likely impact on the aircraft like did it suffer hydraulic failure due to impact and whether it should have flown all the way to Delhi after the episode and not diverted to some nearby airport like Varanasi or Lucknow.DGCA rules stipulate that a pilot testing positive for consumption of psychoactive substances for the first time be referred to for de-addiction and rehabilitation. Such crew member can return for active duties with a negative dope test report.But after resuming flying if the same person tests positive for psychoactive substances again, their licence will be suspended for three years. And if after resuming flying the same person again tests positive for the third time, the flying licence is cancelled.

general secretary KC Venugopal on Sunday urged party leaders to âexercise cautionâ and avoid making remarks that could âplease the BJP.â

Venugopal was responding to questions about Congress leader

âs comments suggesting that Rahul Gandhiâs âChhatron Ki Goonjâ student outreach programme had failed to resonate with Gen Z as much as the Cockroach Janata Party (

)-led protests.

âEven if Congress members do not always strictly abide by party frameworks or discipline, we must be careful to avoid making statements that merely appease the BJP. The BJP will be delighted if someone finds fault with Rahul Gandhi or says two negative things about himâit would be the happiest thing for them,â PTI quoted the Alappuzha MP as saying.

âI have only seen his (Tharoorâs) statement reported by some media channels, as far as I know. I havenât been able to hear exactly what he said. All of us should take care, whether knowingly or unknowinglyâand I donât believe he said it knowingly, nor is he likely to have said it intentionallyâto refrain from making such remarks,â the senior Congress leader added.

World.title: ‘Dialogue, not batons’: Jharkhand CM Soren's message to youth protesting for 'justice' over exam leaks
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

on Sunday urged youths protesting alleged irregularities in recruitment exams not to seek political patronage or allow their agitation to be politicised, saying dialogue, rather than batons, was the way to resolve issues.

"Samvad and not 'lathi-danda-bandook' (dialogue, not batons), can solve all problems," Soren said while addressing the Jharkhand Adivasi Mahotsav in Ranchi.

"Weapons are meant for enemies at the border. I promise the exam protesters that justice will be delivered with full transparency," the chief minister added.

Soren further warned political parties and those with "political ambitions" against misleading the protesting youths through lies and misinformation.

"The stir should not be politicised; I warn those harbouring political ambitions against misguiding youths," he said.

"I urge youths not to seek political patronage (for their stir); justice is your right," Soren added.

The chief minister said the concerns of the protesting students were also his own and assured them that those found guilty of irregularities would face strict action. "Those guilty of irregularities will face strict action.





We caught theft, will deliver justice," he said.

Soren also alleged that vested interests were attempting to disrupt democracy in Jharkhand and accused rival political parties, apparently referring to the BJP, of trying to mislead the state's youth.

World.content:

Congress raises questions over student protests, Amit Shah

Opposition prepares for key Bills in Parliament

Venugopal questions FCRA restrictions, delimitation proposal

NEW DELHI: Congress on Sunday stepped up its opposition to the proposed Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, with AICC general secretary KC Venugopal warning that the party and other opposition parties would strongly protest if the legislation is introduced in Parliament.Venugopal, speaking to reporters in Alappuzha, alleged that the proposed legislation was aimed at targeting minorities and NGOs and said the Opposition would not allow it to be passed."If the Central Government thinks they can cook up and introduce the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill within these two or three days, they should keep that wish to themselves," Venugopal said.He described the proposed legislation as "unconstitutional and anti-people", adding, "We will not allow such an anti-people and unconstitutional bill to be passed."The FCRA Amendment Bill, which seeks to amend the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, is expected to be taken up in the final week of the Monsoon Session.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge also said on Saturday that the party would oppose the measure and that its strategy would be discussed at a meeting of Opposition floor leaders on Monday.Venugopal also sought answers from Union home minister Amit Shah over the alleged use of force against students protesting in Delhi against irregularities in competitive examinations.He asked Shah to respond to allegations concerning the use of pellet guns, lathi charges and tear gas during the protests, and questioned his absence from Parliament."When students in India ask the crucial question of who ordered the use of pellet guns, lathi charges and tear gas shells against them to suppress their protest, Amit Shah would not come forward to answer it," Venugopal said.His remarks came amid a broader opposition campaign over the July 20 protests in Delhi, during which student protesters have alleged excessive use of force.Congress leader Rahul Gandhi had also raised the issue during an interaction with protesters earlier.The Congress' opposition to the FCRA Bill comes ahead of the final three days of the Monsoon Session, with the party issuing a whip asking its MPs to remain present in both Houses on August 10, 11 and 12.Congress chief whip in the Rajya Sabha Jairam Ramesh said the party wanted to ensure that "history should not repeat itself", recalling the suspension of 146 Opposition MPs during the 2023 Winter Session.Ramesh said that after the suspensions, several major pieces of legislation, including the three new criminal laws, were passed with minimal Opposition presence.The Congress has also asked its INDIA bloc allies to ensure their MPs remain present during the final days of the session.The FCRA Bill requires a simple majority for passage, while any Constitution amendment bill on delimitation would require a two-thirds majority, according to the background information provided by the party.Venugopal also questioned the proposed restrictions on organisations receiving foreign contributions and raised the issue of foreign funding received by organisations associated with the RSS."If you have the courage, try controlling the RSS," he said.He also opposed the proposed delimitation legislation, arguing that it could disadvantage states that had successfully implemented population-control measures."This bill effectively chokes states that have successfully implemented population control," Venugopal said, referring to the proposed legislation.On the FCRA Bill, several Opposition parties have expressed concerns. NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule has called for the legislation to either be withdrawn or referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, while DMK president MK Stalin has also urged the Centre to withdraw it.The proposed FCRA legislation has also drawn regional concerns. Mizoram chief minister Lalduhoma said after meeting Shah that he had raised six issues concerning the Bill and received an assurance that the legislation would not be retrospective.Venugopal further criticised the Kerala Police over an alleged defamatory statement by RSS ideologue T G Mohandas concerning the protests, saying an FIR should be followed by an investigation and appropriate action.

World.title: What happens after you apply for an organ transplant?
World.content:
For a patient facing end-stage organ failure, being told that a transplant may be required is only the beginning. The journey from a hospital referral to an actual transplant involves medical evaluation, registration, documentation, waitlist management, organ matching, allocation and, eventually, surgery and long-term follow-up.

In India, the process is coordinated through a network involving the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation (NOTTO), regional and state-level bodies, registered transplant hospitals and transplant coordinators.

The scale of that system has changed sharply. In a February 2026 release, the Press Information Bureau said India recorded nearly 20,000 organ transplants in 2025, compared with fewer than 5,000 in 2013.

More than 1,200 families donated the organs of loved ones after death in 2025, the release said.

Yet the numbers tell only part of the story. Behind every transplant is a sequence that begins long before the surgeon enters the operating theatre â and, for the recipient, often long before an organ is ever offered. Nottoâs says patients are evaluated by a multidisciplinary team, registered through a transplant centre, verified by the relevant allocation body and, once cleared, placed on the appropriate waiting list.





The process starts at the transplant centre

A patient with advanced organ failure is first referred to a licensed transplant centre. Doctors assess the underlying disease, the extent of organ damage and whether transplantation is medically appropriate.

Not every patient with end-stage organ failure will necessarily be fit for transplantation.

Talking about the initial evaluation before transplantation, Dr Manoj Gupta, senior director and HOD, liver transplant, Yatharth Super Speciality Hospital, said, âIt typically includes a review of the patientâs medical history, physical examination, blood and tissue tests, imaging, assessment of organ function, infection screening and evaluation of any underlying conditions.

Eligibility is determined by several factors, including the patientâs overall health, the extent of organ failure, surgical suitability, the likelihood of benefiting from transplantation and the ability to adhere to the post-transplant treatment regimen.

â

However, other factors can also determine eligibility. Dr Goutham Kumar, consultant, HPB & liver transplant services, SPARSH Hospital, added that eligibility also depends on the âabsence of absolute contraindications, including active systemic infections, untreated malignancies, severe substance abuse or irreversible co-morbidities.â

The hospital and transplant coordinator then compile the information required for registration.

Once the application is accepted, the patient's details enter the relevant transplant registry and waiting list. The waiting period can range from the same day to several years.

What being on the waiting list actually means

Being on a transplant waiting list is not simply being in a queue. Notto says patients are listed according to medical criteria, with regular and urgent categories, while priority varies by organ.

For kidney transplants, time on regular dialysis is among the factors considered; other organs follow different criteria.

Dr Kumar explains how these organ-specific criteria work in practice, âLiver allocation often uses the MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score, while heart allocations prioritize patients on mechanical support. Pediatric patients and high-urgency acute cases frequently receive priority.â

Nottoâs manual also provides for urgent or âPriority Oneâ categories for patients meeting organ-specific requirements. Such cases may be reviewed by an expert committee before priority is granted, with hospitals required to provide regular clinical updates.

Registration does not freeze a patientâs status. Their medical condition continues to be monitored and records updated. Depending on their health, a patient may remain active, be made inactive or become medically unfit for transplantation.

Live Kidneys lead Indiaâs transplant numbers

When a donor organ becomes available

The next turn in the journey comes when an organ becomes available. It may come from a living donor, commonly a kidney or part of a liver, or from a deceased donor after certified brain-stem death. At that point, Organ India says, âthe transplant coordinator of the hospital will counsel the family and give them the option of donating organs and tissues.â

The next of kin must consent before retrieval. That makes a donor pledge only at the beginning of the conversation.

Organ India puts it plainly: âIn India it's more important to talk to your family about your decision than it is to pledge your organs and get a donor card.â

Once a donor organ is identified, a rapid, highly coordinated race against time begins. Blood group compatibility and cross-matching are verified between the donor and potential recipient, while the organ is assessed for suitability.

Dr Kumar explains, âA surgical retrieval team harvests the organ and preservation solution is administered.

Transport logisticsâoften utilising dedicated âgreen corridorsâ or air transportâare activated to move the organ immediately.â

The recipient is called to the hospital, re-evaluated and prepared for surgery, with the surgical team ready to proceed as soon as the donor organ arrives.

From brain-stem death to retrieval

A deceased donor is medically maintained while permissions and retrieval arrangements are completed, helping preserve viable organs until they can be recovered.

Once retrieved, however, the clock begins to run: each organ has a limited preservation window.

4â6 hours for heart and lungs, 6â10 hours for intestine, 12â15 hours for liver, 12â24 hours for pancreas and 24â48 hours for kidneys

Cost remains another major barrier to transplantation in India. Dr Kumar said the âinitial surgical costs range from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 35 lakh depending on the organ (kidney vs. liver/heart) and hospital sector (public vs. private).â But the financial burden does not end with the operation. Lifelong immunosuppressants, anti-rejection treatment and âregular diagnostic monitoring add Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000 monthly.

â

That narrow window makes allocation a tightly coordinated process. Organs are assessed, potential recipients identified and transport arranged.

India's transplant numbers are rising

The national system has expanded significantly over the past decade.

The ministry said more than 1,200 families came forward to donate the organs of loved ones after death in 2025.

"More than 4.8 lakh citizens have registered to donate organs and tissues after death through a Aadhaar based verification system, since 17th September 2023," the PIB release said.

The release also said India had developed expertise in complex heart, lung and pancreas transplants and claimed the country "leads the world in hands transplants and performs a greater number of hand transplants than any other country."

The government said the increase reflected improvements in deceased donation, transplant coordination and national organ sharing.

The gap between demand and supply remains

Even after surgery, the process continues. Recipients need lifelong follow-up and immunosuppressive medication, which can also carry long-term risks.

Dr Jagriti Yadav, medical director â lab operations, Cryoviva Life Sciences, said, âThe major long-term risks include acute or chronic graft rejection, opportunistic infections, cardiovascular complications, kidney toxicity, and metabolic side effects related to immunosuppressive medicines.â

The increase in transplant numbers has not eliminated the shortage of organs.

How Indiaâs transplant numbers have surged

A 2024 article published in the National Library of Medicine's PubMed Central noted that India was performing around 17,000-18,000 solid organ transplants a year, making it the world's third-largest transplant country by volume after the United States and China, while transplant rates per million population remained lower than in several high-income countries.

Organ India's data and awareness material has similarly highlighted the disparity between the number of patients requiring organs and the number of deceased donors available. The organisation has estimated that India has a large pool of potential brain-stem-death donors but a much smaller number of actual deceased donors.

For a patient on a waiting list, that gap translates into uncertainty: being medically eligible and registered does not guarantee that a suitable organ will become available in time.

Delhi remains one of the country's major transplant centres.

The Delhi government's organ-donation portal provides information on registered hospitals and transplant services and operates under the Health & Family Welfare Department and the State Appropriate Authority. The department's published information lists registered facilities for kidney, liver, heart, lung and pancreas transplantation, as well as eye and cornea services.

Foreign recipients are also part of the system

Indiaâs transplant system also treats foreign nationals, subject to additional safeguards. Government guidance says an Indian living donor may donate to a foreign recipient only if they are near relatives; donors must be at least 18, with medical-visa and registration requirements applicable to both parties.

Data shows organ transplants for foreign recipients in India

In 2023, India recorded 18,378 transplants and 18,336 individual recipients, including 1,851 foreign nationals, according to Notto data reported in 2024.

Delhi recorded the highest number involving foreign recipients at 1,445, followed by Rajasthan at 116 and West Bengal at 88. Only nine involved unrelated deceased-donor organs.

For a transplant recipient, perhaps the least visible part of the process is the period between registration and an organ offer.

During this period, the patient's condition can change. Tests may have to be repeated, treatment may need adjustment and the transplant centre may update the patient's status on the registry.

The patient therefore remains under the care of the transplant team while the allocation system searches for a medically suitable organ.

Notto says special requests do not guarantee an immediate organ or override the established rules for matching and allocation.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The next stage is a more connected transplant system

Indiaâs transplant system is becoming more digitally connected, with national coordination and data-sharing expanding alongside transplant numbers.

Aadhaar-verified donation registrations crossed 4.8 lakh, while nearly 20,000 transplants were recorded in 2025.

The next challenge is ensuring potential donors are identified, families counselled and organs retrieved, transported and allocated efficiently. For recipients, that means staying medically fit, updating the transplant centre and following clinical advice.

World.title: ‘Stones, shoes thrown at my car’: Mamata faces protest during visit to kin of dead TMC worker

on Sunday alleged that her car was pelted with stones after protesters intercepted her convoy while she was visiting the family of deceased

World.title: An appointment with the Pen Doctor, who revives old fountain pens with love and expertise in Madurai
World.content:
Long before disposable pens became common, people brought their favourite fountain pens to R Srinivasan whenever they stopped writing. They still do. Everyone fondly calls him the ‘Pen Doctor’. He is more than 70 years old and has been repairing fountain pens from his small shop near the Meenakshi Amman Temple for more than 50 years. From old models such as Pilot and Wality to newer China-made models, his collection shows how fountain pens have changed over the years. While most of us would throw away a pen that has stopped writing, Srinivasan repairs it and gives it new life.

His small shop is easy to miss if you are walking through the busy streets around the temple. But for those who still love writing with fountain pens, it’s a familiar spot.

Srinivasan learned how to fix fountain pens from his father. “I have been doing this for almost 50 years,” he says. “My father taught me everything. I learned by watching him and helping him.”

Every day, people walk into his shop with fountain pens that have stopped writing. Some have bent nibs, while others have dried-up ink or broken parts. Before repairing a pen, the Pen Doctor takes a close look at it to find out what the problem is.

“Every pen is different. Some can be repaired in a few minutes, while others take time,” he says.

Although use-and-throw pens have become common, there are still many people who prefer fountain pens. Students, teachers, office-goers and pen collectors continue to visit his shop. Some come to repair an old pen they have been using for years, while others buy fountain pens from his collection, which includes old brands as well as newer ones.

But business isn’t what it used to be. “Nowadays, most people buy a new pen if the old one stops working,” he says.

The shop is busiest when schools reopen in June, as students throng the shop.

“Some office-goers who came to my shop years ago are now retired. Even now, they come back because they still enjoy writing with fountain pens,” he says.

With a few simple tools and years of experience, he patiently cleans the pen, adjusts the nib and gets it back to writing again. For many customers, these pens remind them of their school days, a loved one or a special gift. That is why they choose to repair them instead of throwing them away.

Even though people now use computers, mobile phones and tablets for most of their writing, Srinivasan believes fountain pens will always have their own place. He fondly recalls repairing Writer pens, one of the most popular brands of its time and among the earliest fountain pens used by many people.

He says he repairs and sells a wide range of fountain pens, including Parker, Japanese, German, American Parker, C4, Swan and Waterman models. He also proudly shows a set of ‘Kalaignar’ pens, which, he says, are the same model once used by former Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M Karunanidhi. The pens in his collection are priced between ₹100 and ₹500.

Fountain pen collector M Balamurugan says he has been visiting Srinivasan’s shop for years. “I enjoy collecting fountain pens, and this is one of the few places where I can still find old and rare models. Every time I visit, he has something different to show. He knows almost everything about fountain pens, and that is what keeps me coming back,” he says.

Time may have changed the way people write, but it has not changed the Pen Doctor’s love for fountain pens. Every day, he continues to repair old pens with the same patience he learnt from his father, proving that some things are still worth fixing instead of replacing.

World.title: 63-year-old ragpicker arrested for murdering wife in Bengaluru
World.content:
The Bengaluru police have arrested a 63-year-old man for allegedly murdering his wife in southeast Bengaluru’s Vivek Nagar on Friday night (August 7).

The accused has been identified as Jerry Anthony, a ragpicker. He allegedly strangled his wife, Geetha, 50, and fled from the scene. According to the police, both were ragpickers and had married about six years ago. The couple used to live in an abandoned vehicle near the Austin Town BDA complex.

A preliminary police probe revealed that around 9.30 p.m. on Friday, Anthony and Geetha went to Vivek Nagar to collect scrap materials near a garbage blackspot on 4th Main Road connecting to Ejipura Main Road. While Geetha was segregating garbage, Anthony allegedly strangled her with her veil before fleeing the spot.

An investigator in the case said Anthony claimed that Geetha had a drinking habit and would pick fights every day. Even on Friday, she allegedly picked a fight with Anthony after drinking, which led to the incident.

The Vivek Nagar police have booked Anthony under Section 103 of the BNS and have arrested him.
